entries.short: Cuba skips fall-back: Havana off on old tz data
entries.title: Cuba keeps daylight saving time: time zone data older than 2026f shows America/Havana an hour behind from 1 November
entries.what: On 24 October Cuba announced that it would not set its clocks back on 1 November 2026 and stays on UTC−04 until 7 November 2027. Software on older data switches America/Havana to UTC−05 at 05:00 UTC on 1 November and shows Cuban times one hour behind until 14 March 2027.

An XML file that names an XSL stylesheet in its opening lines (<?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" …?>) is then no longer turned into a styled page: readers see the raw XML or an almost empty page. Chrome Beta, Dev and Canary have had XSLT off by default since Chrome 145.
entries.affected: People who open these XML pages in Chrome, not the programs that read them: crawlers and OAI-PMH harvesters fetch the XML itself, so the removal does not change what they get. The common cases are styled sitemaps and the OAI-PMH endpoints of research repositories. On 9 October 2026 we found an XSL-styled sitemap on 122 of the 2,642 most popular sites on the Tranco list (we checked /sitemap.xml, /sitemap_index.xml and /wp-sitemap.xml), and an XSLT stylesheet line on 480 of the first 1,500 repository endpoints in an October 2025 copy of the Open Archives Initiative registry (32%). We then opened the first 80 eligible sites from each list, in list order. Of those 160, 5 failed to load and 4 were blank even with XSLT on, which leaves 151. With XSLT off, the text of 149 of the 151 no longer matched the normal page: a similarity score that compares the words in order, where 1 means the same text, fell below 0.5. We did not measure web pages that run XSLT from JavaScript (XSLTProcessor) or Android apps that show pages in a WebView.
entries.check: Open your sitemap or other styled XML page in Chrome Beta, Dev or Canary, which already have XSLT off, or quit Chrome and start it again with the switch below, which is how we ran our test. If you see raw XML or a nearly empty page, the page is affected. To find the files, search your site's XML for the stylesheet line; a sitemap made by a plugin may exist only at its web address, so open that too.
entries.checkCode:
# Chrome switch that turns XSLT off:
--disable-features=XSLT

# XML files with a stylesheet line:
grep -rln --include='*.xml' \
  'xml-stylesheet' .

fix.text: For XML pages that people read, add Chrome's polyfill, which runs XSLT in JavaScript and WebAssembly: put xslt-polyfill.min.js from the xslt-polyfill package on your site, then add the element below as the first thing inside the root element, straight after its start tag. In our 9 October 2026 test (Chrome for Testing headless shell 153.0.8010.12 with XSLT switched off to stand in for Chrome 158, and xslt-polyfill 1.0.31), 148 of the 151 pages scored 0.95 or more on that similarity score (98%). Executed by us; not independently reproduced. Those 151 pages were taken in list order and leave out pages that failed or were already blank, so 98% is not a success rate for the web as a whole. We compared text, not layout: most pages move from quirks mode to standards mode, so check spacing and widths by eye. Snags we hit: a root element that closes itself, such as <sitemapindex …/>, needs a separate end tag first; the script must be served as UTF-8, or its built-in WebAssembly fails to load; and stylesheets on another site must allow cross-origin reads (CORS). Take care with XML that programs read. The element becomes part of what crawlers and harvesters receive, and when we checked, it made otherwise valid sitemap, sitemap index and OAI-PMH files fail validation against their published schemas. We did not test real crawlers or harvesters, so add it there only after you have checked that the changed XML, and the programs that read it, accept it. Where that XML must stay valid, leave it as it is and give people a separate HTML page made by running the XSLT on your server, one of the routes on Chrome's page; readers can also add the XSLT browser extension that Chrome's page describes. A sitemap needs no styling for search engines: deleting its stylesheet line keeps every URL, and people then see the XML unstyled.
fix.code:
<script
src="/xslt-polyfill.min.js"
xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
></script>

entries.short: postgres:latest becomes 19
entries.title: postgres:latest becomes 19: unpinned stacks stop starting
entries.what: PostgreSQL 19 is planned for 19 November 2026 (release candidate 2 on 12 November). When it ships, the official Docker image's postgres, postgres:latest, postgres:alpine, postgres:trixie, postgres:bookworm, postgres:alpine3.24 and postgres:alpine3.23 tags move from 18 to 19. A stack that uses one of those tags and already holds data will not start once it pulls the new image and recreates the database container. In our test the 19 container exited with code 1 ("Error: in 18+ … there appears to be PostgreSQL data in /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker", or "database files are incompatible with server" when PGDATA is set).
entries.affected: Self-hosted stacks that already hold data and use postgres, postgres:latest, postgres:alpine, postgres:trixie, postgres:bookworm, postgres:alpine3.24 or postgres:alpine3.23 (directly or through a registry mirror) without an @sha256 digest. Of 253 projects on the awesome-selfhosted list whose main compose file uses the official postgres image (278 counting test, dev and CI files), 31 use a tag that will move. We then narrowed this to the files a user is likely to copy, after seeing the scan. 9 of those match the two layouts that failed in our test, so existing installs will stop once they pull and recreate on or after 19 November: cal.diy, Hyperswitch, Payload's with-postgres template, Reactive Resume, Grist's Keycloak example, Retrom, Bracket, BookLogr and PodFetch. 4 of these 9 merged a change that moved the volume mount for PostgreSQL 18 (October 2025 to August 2026) and kept the moving tag. We read each project's compose files at its head on 19 October 2026; we did not read every install or run the projects themselves.
entries.check: Run this in the folder with your compose file. A line printed means that service moves to 19 on 19 November; it resolves ${VARIABLES} first and also catches mirrors such as public.ecr.aws/docker/library/postgres. For a service with build: instead of image:, read its Dockerfile FROM line: FROM postgres with no number, or with one of the tags above, moves too.

fix.text: Pin the major your database runs today: postgres:18 if it runs 18 (or 18-alpine, 18-trixie, 18-bookworm). We tested this with two 1,000-row 18.6 databases, one in the default layout and one with PGDATA set: 19 RC 1 refused both, and both opened again on postgres:18 with all 1,000 rows. Upgrade to 19 later with pg_upgrade or a dump and restore. Do not run docker compose down -v as a fix: it can delete the database volume.
fix.code: image: postgres:18

entries.short: NOAA ends NAM: forecast downloads stop
entries.title: NOAA ends the NAM weather model: downloads stop
entries.what: On or after 3 November 2026 at 12:00 UTC, NOAA's NCEP stops running the NAM, SREF, HREF and HiresW forecast models and NAM MOS (HiresW Guam continues). NOAA has moved this date three times since its first notice in May. If 3 November is declared a Critical Weather Day or an Enhanced Caution Event, or significant weather is expected, the change moves to 12:00 UTC on the next weekday that is not a Critical Weather Day and has no significant weather. The files under nomads.ncep.noaa.gov/pub/data/nccf/com/{nam,sref,href,hiresw,nam_mos}/prod/, the matching NOMADS grib filters, and the feeds that mirror them stop getting new runs. RRFS and REFS replace them on the same day.
entries.affected: Scripts, apps and models that download NAM-family forecasts in real time. On 19 October 2026, our GitHub scan found NAM-family download-path matches in 85 active public repositories (pushed since 19 October 2025); 50 of them had no RRFS mention in the files scanned. We then read those 50 matches, using rules written after seeing the scan: 28 had code, not a test or a comment, that builds or requests a NAM-family download path (24 codebases, counting copies of the same code once). They include open-meteo, Iowa Environmental Mesonet scripts, WindNinja, BC Wildfire Predictive Services, wrfxpy, SCHISM utilities and RASP soaring forecasts. We did not run any of this code, and some of these paths may already be out of use. The scan covered default branches without forks and left out 12 very large repositories and some large files, so it does not count every NAM user; a project that mentions RRFS has not necessarily switched.
entries.check: From your repository root, search for NAM-family download addresses. Read each match: code that reads past dates, for example from the AWS noaa-nam-pds archive, does not need new NAM runs. Code that asks for a fresh run gets no new NAM run after the retirement, and a “latest” or “Best” lookup may return old data instead of an error.

fix.text: Choose the replacement for the product you use: RRFS for NAM and HiresW, REFS for HREF (NOAA lists SREF as replaced by the two together), then check its domain, grid, lead times and fields. Both are already published at nomads.ncep.noaa.gov/pub/data/nccf/com/rrfs/para/ and refs/para/, which NOAA's notice moves to rrfs/prod/ and refs/prod/ when the change takes effect; RRFS is also in the AWS bucket noaa-rrfs-ops-pds. RRFS surface fields are in the 2dfld files (rrfs.tCCz.2dfld.3km.fFFF.conus.grib2); prslev holds pressure levels. The CONUS 3 km grid reaches only the southern edge of British Columbia; for British Columbia, use the Alaska 3 km (ak) or North America 13 km (na) files. On 19 October NOMADS had no RRFS grib filter; the .idx files allow byte-range downloads. In one cycle's file lists (NAM 12 km awphys12, 19 October 00Z, against RRFS 3 km prslev and 2dfld, 18 October 00Z, both f012), 2 m temperature, dew point and humidity, 10 m wind, gust, precipitation, reflectivity and CAPE keep their GRIB names, but a matching name does not prove a field can be swapped in. Precipitation comes as two records per file, the last hour and the run total, not NAM's 3- and 12-hour buckets. There is no PRMSL (RRFS provides MSLET; check it meets your needs) and no ACPCP, and soil comes at 9 depths instead of NAM's 4 layers, so WRF's Vtable.NAM cannot read it unchanged. We compared files only and did not run this switch against any project's code.

entries.short: LaunchDarkly retires old REST API versions
entries.title: LaunchDarkly REST API: old versions stop working
entries.what: LaunchDarkly retires every REST API version except 20240415 on 31 December 2026, in a window from 09:00 to 17:00 UTC (01:00 to 09:00 PST). Its notice says that after this date, all requests made to retired versions will stop working. Version 20240415 pages its list calls: List feature flags returns 20 flags unless you ask for more (limit goes up to 100), and the lists of segments, custom roles, access tokens and workflows page too. This is the REST API only; LaunchDarkly says no SDKs are being deprecated.
entries.affected: Scripts and integrations that call app.launchdarkly.com/api/v2 with an LD-API-Version header older than 20240415, or with no header and an access token set to an older version, stop working on 31 December. Code that moves to 20240415 without paging gets only the first page of each list: 20 flags by default, with no error. New access tokens default to 20240415, so a feature-flag list call with no header and no limit returns at most 20 flags. LaunchDarkly's generated API clients (launchdarkly-api for Python, api-client-go for Go) need version 21 or later to use 20240415.
entries.check: From your repository root, search for REST API calls and generated clients. Every call should send LD-API-Version: 20240415, and every list call should repeat with offset raised by limit until items comes back empty. Code that builds the URL from its own base variable will not match the first search; look for it by hand.

fix.text: Send the header on every call and page through each list. The code below lists every flag in a project in Python and needs the Requests package installed (pip install requests); PROJECT is your project key and TOKEN your access token. Segments (limit up to 50), custom roles and access tokens page the same way. We tested it only on a local mock of the paging LaunchDarkly documents, not on LaunchDarkly's servers: with 57 flags, a single 20240415 request returned 20 and this loop returned all 57; with 250 flags it returned all 250, 100 at a time.
fix.code:
import requests

url = "https://app.launchdarkly.com"
url += f"/api/v2/flags/{PROJECT}"
headers = {
    "Authorization": TOKEN,
    "LD-API-Version": "20240415",
}
flags, offset = [], 0
while True:
    q = {"limit": 100,
         "offset": offset}
    r = requests.get(
        url, params=q,
        headers=headers)
    r.raise_for_status()
    items = r.json()["items"]
    if not items:
        break
    flags += items
    offset += 100

entries.short: Homebrew removes node@18
entries.title: Homebrew removes node@18, and icu4c@77 stops it installing the same day
entries.what: Homebrew disabled node@18 on 29 October 2025, but it still installs with a warning, because it is also marked deprecated. Homebrew's docs say disabled formulae are removed automatically one year after their disable date, so node@18 and hasura-cli are due to go from 30 October 2026, and tldr, disabled on 24 October 2025, from 25 October. The three removals we watched this month (vera++, cloudiscovery and phpmd) each landed the day after that anniversary, and so did tldr: Homebrew removed it at 00:20 UTC on 25 October. Also on 30 October, Homebrew disables icu4c@77, which node@18 depends on. icu4c@77 has no deprecation date of its own, so this one blocks: we ran brew install node@18 on Linux with Homebrew 7.0.10 and the clock set to 31 October, and it failed with "icu4c@77 has been disabled". A second agent reran it on the same machine and got the same result. On 28 October we ran it again with Homebrew 7.0.11 and the clock at 31 October, together with brew install dotnet@6, brew install postgresql@12 and a Brewfile line for icu4c@77; all four failed with the same error. We did not run them on macOS. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: CI jobs, setup scripts and Brewfiles that install node@18, hasura-cli or tldr. Once a formula is removed, brew install fails with "No available formula with the name"; brew bundle reports the failure and installs the rest of the Brewfile. A Brewfile line for icu4c@77 itself failed the same way with the clock at 31 October, and brew bundle still installed the rest of that Brewfile. GitHub code search found a brew "icu4c@77" line in at least 89 public repositories and a brew "node@18" line in at least 54, mostly dotfiles; it counted repositories pushed to in the last year and not archived, on default branches, leaving out forks. Homebrew's formula data lists three formulae that depend on icu4c@77: node@18, dotnet@6 and postgresql@12. dotnet@6 and postgresql@12 are not due to leave until mid-November, but with the clock at 31 October neither would install. A machine that already has node@18 keeps working: in a second run with the clock at 31 October, node@18 still ran, and brew upgrade, brew bundle install and brew reinstall node@18 succeeded, because icu4c@77 was already installed. The trap is brew uninstall node@18: it also removed icu4c@77 and 17 other dependencies nothing else needed, and brew install node@18 then failed. Homebrew counted 463 node@18, 494 hasura-cli and 1,204 tldr installs in the 30 days to 19 October. These are install events, CI runners included, not users.
entries.check: From your repository root, list what your CI and Brewfile install with Homebrew, then look up each name's disable_date and deprecation_date in Homebrew's formula data, as below. A disable_date means the formula is scheduled to leave homebrew/core one year after it; in the removals we watched, it went the day after the anniversary. If deprecation_date is null, the formula is not also marked deprecated, and in our runs such formulae stopped installing on the disable date itself; icu4c@77 did, with the clock set to 31 October. A null disable_date means no removal is scheduled yet. Do not go by brew info alone: it can print "It will be disabled on …" for a formula with no disable date set, so that line does not give a removal date. A name that is not in homebrew/core returns an error, and this schedule does not cover it. Installs that build the name from a variable will not match the search; look for them by hand.
entries.checkCode:
grep -rnE 'brew install|^ *brew "' \
  .github Brewfile
A=https://formulae.brew.sh/api
P='"d[a-z]*_date":[^,]*'
L="node@18 hasura-cli tldr icu4c@77"
for N in $L; do
  printf '%s ' "$N"
  curl -fsSL "$A/formula/$N.json" |
    grep -oE "$P" | tr '\n' ' '
  echo
done

fix.text: Move to node@24 (brew install node@24) or to node, the current release, and run your own tests on it; we did not test whether a given project works there. Do not move to node@22: Homebrew marks it deprecated from 30 October 2026, and it is due to be disabled a year later. For tldr, Homebrew names tlrc as the replacement. Until you have moved, do not run brew uninstall node@18 on a machine that has it. Copying node@18 alone into your own tap, as in the 9 January protobuf@21 entry, stops working on 30 October: with the clock at 31 October it failed on the disabled icu4c@77. What worked, on Linux with Homebrew 7.0.11 and the clock at 31 October, took three more steps: copy icu4c@77 into the same tap without its deprecate! and disable! lines; change node@18's line to depends_on "<your tap>/icu4c@77"; and run brew trust <your tap> once. brew install <your tap>/node@18 then installed v18.20.8 from bottles, with ICU 77. Without the changed line, node@18 still took icu4c@77 from homebrew/core; without brew trust, Homebrew refused to load the tap's icu4c@77. A one-formula tap such as the protobuf@21 one needs no trust step, because installing a formula by its tap name trusts it. Once node@18 leaves homebrew/core, take both files from its git history. We did not run this on macOS. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.

entries.short: Chrome 157 builds in the HTTP-only warning
entries.title: Chrome 157 builds in the HTTP-only site warning, reaching fleets that limit Google's config
entries.what: Chrome stops on a warning page before it opens a public site that has no working HTTPS, and asks the person before loading it over plain HTTP. People can click through. Google says Chrome will not keep warning about an insecure site that someone visits regularly, so the stop falls on first and occasional visits. Most Chrome users already have this: Google's server-side config for Stable Chrome turns it on for desktop Chrome 154 and later (Android 155 and later), as we read that config on 20 October 2026. Chrome 157 reaches the Stable channel on 3 November 2026 (an early release to a small share of users starts on 21 October) and builds the same default into its code. That brings it to browsers where an administrator has set the ChromeVariations policy to limit or turn off Google's config. In our test, Chrome 155 with that policy opened both of our HTTP test sites without asking, and Chrome Beta 157 with the same policy stopped both (Google Chrome on Linux, one run each; Windows, macOS, Android and ChromeOS not tested).
entries.affected: Public sites still served only over http:// on the normal port, and the people who open them for the first time or after a long gap. The people new to the warning on 3 November use Chrome with ChromeVariations set to critical fixes only (1) or off (2). Chrome's own list of its 1 million most visited sites (Chrome UX Report, September 2026) has 7,748 sites with an http:// address. On 20 October 2026 we opened 1,002 of them, each in a new profile with no Google config applied, in Chrome 155 and in Chrome 157: all 502 in the top 100,000 and 500 of the rest, picked at random. Of the sites that loaded over HTTP in Chrome 155, Chrome 157 stopped 93% in the top 100,000 (278 of 300) and 89% of the rest (288 of 322). Across the whole list, that is about 4,450 of the top 1 million sites (between 4,110 and 4,780) that stop a first-time visitor. Sites we could not reach from our network (19.6% of those we opened) count as not stopped, so the figure may be low. Executed by us (Chrome for Testing 157.0.8103.6 on Linux, one network location); not independently reproduced. Not stopped: sites on another port, such as http://host:8080 (all 33 that opened over HTTP in Chrome 155 opened in Chrome 157 with no warning), and sites whose HTTPS works, which Chrome opens over HTTPS without asking. We counted sites on a first visit, not warnings per person. We did not test Windows, macOS, phones, intranet sites (Google says private sites are left out), Wi-Fi sign-in pages or mobile carriers' HTTP-only billing pages.
entries.check: Open your site's http:// address in a current Chrome on default settings. If a warning page appears instead of your site, new visitors see it too. If your organisation restricts ChromeVariations, use Chrome Beta (version 157 or later) with a new profile and Google's config turned off; the command below does this on Linux and is close to how we ran our test.

# Chrome Beta with a new profile:
google-chrome-beta \
  --user-data-dir="$(mktemp -d)" \
  --disable-field-trial-config \
  http://your-site.example/

fix.text: For a public site, serve it over HTTPS on port 443; Chrome opens sites whose HTTPS works over HTTPS with no warning. For computers your organisation manages, while sites move to HTTPS, you can set the Chrome policy HttpsOnlyMode to disallowed (below; on Linux, a JSON file in /etc/opt/chrome/policies/managed/). entries.short: Rust 1.100: a few version checks misread it
entries.title: Rust 1.100.0 becomes stable: scripts that compare versions as text call it too old
entries.what: Rust 1.100.0 is due to become the stable release on 12 November 2026, the first with a three-digit minor version. A script that compares the rustc version as text or as a decimal number reads 1.100 as older than 1.99, because "1.1" sorts before "1.9" and 1.100 is 1.1 as a decimal, so it stops with a "Rust too old" error. Comparing each part as a whole number accepts it. We ran five text or decimal checks and five whole-number checks against the version strings of rustc 1.99.1, the current 1.100.0 beta and a stable 1.100.0 string we wrote ourselves, since stable is not out yet. All ten accepted 1.99.1; the five text or decimal checks rejected both 1.100 strings, and the five whole-number checks accepted them. We ran them on Linux, and the PowerShell checks in PowerShell 7, not Windows PowerShell 5.1. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Shell, Python, PowerShell and Makefile scripts that read the rustc version and compare it with a minimum version as text or as a decimal. In public GitHub code we found few. Code search returned 3,184 files that read the rustc version near the words minimum, MSRV or too old. Model labellers sorted them, and we ran every check they labelled as failing: at least 215 distinct checks compare the version safely, and 14 distinct scripts, in 61 repositories, reject 1.100. Only 3 of those scripts are in repositories that are not archived and were pushed to in the last 6 months, 5 repositories in all. Most of the 14 are copies of the Windows installer from rustlings 5 and earlier (install.ps1), which prints "Rust version is too old"; one active copy is in the Rust course sunface/rust-course, though its README does not tell readers to run it. Code search ranks best matches and leaves out forks and checks without those words, so these counts are lower bounds for this search, not a rate for all Rust projects. We did not search build scripts of crates on crates.io. The Rust project uses Crater to build and test many crates against each beta, but that does not cover every crate or configuration.
entries.check: From your repository root, list the scripts that read the rustc version, as below, and look at how each one compares it with its minimum. Text comparison (the < test inside [[ ]] in bash, -lt or -gt on strings in PowerShell), decimal comparison (awk, bc, float() in Python) and reading fixed character positions misread 1.100. To try a script before 12 November, run it under rustup's beta toolchain, which already reports the 1.100.0 beta. In our run on Linux, rustup run beta made a text check fail and a sort -V check pass. Checks that read the version through cargo or a variable will not match the search; look for them by hand. The grep only reads files. The next commands download and install the beta toolchain, then run your build script: replace ./build.sh with a build command you trust, and run it in your normal test environment.
entries.checkCode:
grep -rnIE 'rustc +(-vV|-V|--version)' \
  --exclude-dir=target \
  --exclude-dir=.git .
rustup toolchain install beta \
  --profile minimal
rustup run beta ./build.sh

fix.text: Compare the version parts as whole numbers. Take the version from rustc's output, drop any beta or nightly suffix, and compare with sort -V in a shell, [version] in PowerShell or a tuple of integers in Python, as below for a 1.70 minimum. In our runs on Linux, with GNU sort 9.4, Python 3.12 and PowerShell 7.4, each rejected 1.69.0 and accepted 1.70.0, 1.99.1, the 1.100.0 beta, a stable 1.100.0 string and a 1.101.0 nightly. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
# bash
V=$(rustc --version | cut -d' ' -f2)
V=${V%%-*}
printf '%s\n' 1.70.0 "$V" |
  sort -V -C || exit 1
# PowerShell
$v = (rustc --version).Split(" ")[1]
$v = [version]($v -replace "-.*")
if ($v -lt [version]"1.70") {exit 1}
# Python (v = the version text)
import sys
v = v.split("-")[0]
n = tuple(map(int, v.split(".")))
if n < (1, 70): sys.exit("too old")

entries.short: GitHub SSH brownout: old RSA clients fail
entries.time: on those two days only; GitHub has not announced the hours
entries.title: GitHub SSH brownouts: old clients with RSA keys fail on 4 November and 9 December
entries.what: On 4 November and 9 December 2026, github.com runs brownouts of a change it makes permanent on 13 January 2027: it stops accepting RSA signatures made with SHA-1 (ssh-rsa) and the diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 key exchange. GitHub has not announced the hours or how long each brownout lasts. Only Git over SSH is affected: GitHub says remotes that start with https:// are not. In our own test, against a stand-in for GitHub's server, 10 of 32 SSH client stacks broke, all only with an RSA key. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Two parts of the change can break a connection to github.com over SSH. The first is SHA-1 signatures, which some old clients are limited to when they use an RSA key. Since 15 March 2022, GitHub has required SHA-2 signatures for RSA keys added on or after 2 November 2021. The SHA-1 removal therefore newly affects only older RSA keys used with SHA-1 signatures. A working RSA connection alone does not tell you the key's age. The second is the key exchange. The key-exchange removal can affect a client that has no other key exchange in common with GitHub, regardless of the key's type or age. In our test, CentOS 7's libssh2 1.8.0 failed that way, because the one being removed is the only one it shares with github.com. Git's own ssh command is usually OpenSSH, which GitHub lists as fine from 7.2p1. The breaks we found were in programs that use a library instead: Python code with paramiko, Node code with ssh2, Java with JSch, Go with x/crypto/ssh, PuTTY's plink, and curl or other programs built on libssh2. That includes Debian 12's libssh2, and Debian 12 has long-term support until 30 June 2028. On GitHub Enterprise Server the change comes with version 3.25 instead. To test it, we set our own OpenSSH 10.0 server to github.com's current SSH algorithm lists, removed those two, and connected from 35 client stacks with RSA, ECDSA and Ed25519 keys, twice each; 32 of them worked before the removal. 10 of those 32 broke, all only with the RSA key: PuTTY 0.70 and 0.73 (Ubuntu 18.04 and 20.04), paramiko 2.4.2 and 2.8.1, node ssh2 0.8.9 and 1.0.0, the original JSch 0.1.55 (com.jcraft), Go x/crypto from 17 November 2021, and curl with libssh2 1.10.0 (Debian 12) and 1.8.0 (CentOS 7). All five OpenSSH clients we tested kept working. The newest versions we tried of paramiko, node ssh2, Go x/crypto, Ruby net-ssh, PuTTY and libssh2 passed too, and so did the maintained JSch fork com.github.mwiede, unlike the original com.jcraft JSch 0.1.55, the only original JSch version we tried. Every break was below a minimum version in GitHub's table, or was an old version of a library the table does not list. This was our stand-in, not GitHub's server; we will check github.com during the 4 November brownout. We did not test Windows clients, TeamCity, JGit, libgit2 builds, Dropbear or ssh-agent setups. Executed by us; not independently reproduced. Update, 4 November: from our location, github.com was in the brownout from about 08:30 to 22:00 UTC (we checked every 30 minutes). During it, curl with CentOS 7's libssh2 1.8.0 failed with "curl: (2) Failure establishing ssh session", and old paramiko waited about 40 seconds before printing a misleading key-file error. The other old clients printed the same errors as in our earlier test. We tested with a key GitHub did not know, and we will check again on 9 December.
entries.check: Only remotes that do not start with https:// matter, and git remote -v lists them. ssh-add -l shows the type of each key in your SSH agent, in brackets at the end of its line; ssh-keygen -lf followed by a key file does the same for a key on disk. Ed25519 and ECDSA avoid the SHA-1 RSA change; the client still needs a supported key exchange. So whatever the key, find what makes the connection and its version. The next commands print the installed paramiko, ssh2 and Go x/crypto versions, PuTTY's version and the libssh2 version your curl uses; run each where that tool or project is installed. For Java, look for jsch in mvn dependency:tree or gradle dependencies. Compare the versions with the fix below. A program that bundles its own SSH library will not show up here.
entries.checkCode:
git remote -v
ssh-add -l
pip show paramiko | grep Version
npm ls ssh2
go list -m golang.org/x/crypto
plink -V
curl -V | grep -o 'libssh2/[0-9.]*'

fix.text: Switch to an Ed25519 or ECDSA key. In our test it worked on every stack that can load one, old versions included, and GitHub says these keys keep working. Make one as below, add the .pub file to GitHub as an SSH key or a deploy key, and point your tool at it. The original JSch 0.1.55 loads ECDSA keys but not Ed25519. Or upgrade the client. These versions passed with an RSA key: paramiko 2.9.0, ssh2 1.17.0, the JSch fork com.github.mwiede 0.1.66, Go x/crypto v0.1.0, PuTTY 0.76 and libssh2 1.11.1. GitHub's table asks for Go x/crypto 0.16.0 and PuTTY 0.82, so aim for those or later. CentOS 7's libssh2 1.8.0 loads neither key type, so it has no key workaround: move that job to a newer system. Tested on 21 October against our stand-in server, not GitHub's. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 \
  -f ~/.ssh/github_ed25519
cat ~/.ssh/github_ed25519.pub

entries.short: Ruby 4.1 (expected): old native gems fail
entries.time: expected (Ruby's usual Christmas release; not announced)
entries.title: Ruby 4.1 (expected 25 December): gems with old C extensions stop installing
entries.what: Ruby 4.1.0 is expected on 25 December 2026. Every new Ruby version from 3.0 in 2020 to 4.0 in 2025 came out on 25 December, but Ruby has not announced this date. Ruby 4.1 removes C functions that have been deprecated for years, among them the untyped data-object functions such as Data_Wrap_Struct and Data_Get_Struct, the taint macros and rb_iterate, so gems whose native extension still uses them stop installing or loading. We attempted installs and three candidate require names for 165 native-extension gems among the top 3,000 by all-time downloads, using an October 2026 snapshot. Twenty-two installed on Ruby 4.0.7 and showed a build, load or native-extension regression on 4.1.0-preview1; this includes atomic's fallback to pure Ruby. We expect 21 of these regressions on the final release, seven among the top 1,000: eventmachine, thin, kostya-sigar, yajl-ruby, hiredis, therubyracer and ffi-yajl. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Apps and images that install one of these gems on Ruby 4.1. Besides the seven above, they are cbor, timfel-krb5-auth, atomic, iconv, hpricot, rblineprof, zookeeper, ruby-stemmer, panko_serializer, algorithms, ruby-debug-ide, debase, bson_ext and numo-narray. Most fail at gem install with a compile error. panko_serializer and rblineprof install, then fail at require with "undefined symbol: Data_Wrap_Struct". atomic loaded after warning that it was using its pure-Ruby implementation; we did not measure its speed. thin fails through eventmachine and ruby-debug-ide through debase; bson_ext, debase and numo-narray break on other changes to Ruby's C interface. rinku failed with "undefined symbol: ruby_abi_version". Ruby's abi.h says released versions do not define this preview ABI number, so we infer this failure will not affect the final release; we did not test a final-release build. We exclude rinku from the 21 expected regressions. Two more changes reach apps without these gems. tsort moves from a default gem to a bundled gem, so under bundle exec it must be in the resolved bundle, either directly or through a dependency. Without it, our preview probes for molinillo 0.8.0, mobility 1.3.2, packwerk 3.3.1 and facter 2.5.7 raised "cannot load such file -- tsort". CocoaPods 1.17.0 installs that molinillo without tsort; we did not run CocoaPods itself. And for 14 of the 26 popular gems that ship ready-built Linux binaries, the latest x86_64 Linux binary metadata excludes Ruby 4.1: nokogiri, ffi, pg, google-protobuf, prism, grpc, sqlite3, commonmarker, prometheus-client-mmap, re2, gitlab-glfm-markdown, tiny_tds, code_ownership and tiktoken_ruby. A compatible source package may be selected instead; building it requires a compiler and any required development libraries. Official Ruby slim images omit build tools by default, so check your build environment before upgrading. We attempted source installs and three candidate require names in the official ruby:4.0.7 and ruby:4.1.0-preview1 images on Linux x86_64 with GCC 12. The protocol accepts a successful install when none of the three names loads on either version; 17 of the 118 gems with no detected regression had that limitation. Twenty-one gems failed on the baseline too, for mixed reasons including version constraints, API errors and missing libraries; four builds timed out. Those results do not establish Ruby 4.1 compatibility. We tested latest releases, not older locked versions, and preview1, not final. The baseline packwerk and facter probes ended with unrelated private-constant and wrong-path errors after reaching the tsort warning; their preview LoadErrors diagnose the missing tsort, not a complete application test. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: Run this in the folder with your Gemfile.lock; it only reads the file. It prints each of the 21 gems, and molinillo, mobility, packwerk and facter, that your lockfile installs; gems you already pinned with a git line show up too. For the tsort error, a tsort gem spec in the resolved bundle can satisfy this dependency; a mention of tsort alone does not prove that it is available to the running bundle. Also look for the 14 gems with ready-built binaries if you build on an official Ruby slim image.

  kostya-sigar yajl-ruby hiredis \
  therubyracer ffi-yajl cbor \
  timfel-krb5-auth atomic iconv \
  hpricot rblineprof zookeeper \
  ruby-stemmer panko_serializer \
  algorithms ruby-debug-ide \
  debase bson_ext numo-narray \
  molinillo mobility packwerk \
  facter; do
  grep -nE "^ {4}$g \(" Gemfile.lock
done

fix.text: Upgrade each gem when its maintainers release a fix. eventmachine, thin, yajl-ruby and panko_serializer have fixed this on their main branch but not released it; eventmachine's last release was in May 2018. Until then, pin the fixed source: copy the lines below for the gems you use into your Gemfile, replacing their existing gem lines, and run bundle install. thin needs both the thin and the eventmachine lines; with only the eventmachine line, thin 2.0.1 still fails. A git pin is a stopgap: it needs git at install time, and it installs code that is not a rubygems.org release. For the tsort error, add gem "tsort", the last line below; that fixed molinillo and mobility. For the other 17 gems we have no tested fix. Our source scan found removed-API identifiers in 12 default-branch checkouts, which we did not build; ruby-debug-ide depends on debase; and our metadata lookup found no GitHub source repository for four gems. Replace them, or stay on Ruby 4.0 until a fixed release ships. We tested each fix on 4.1.0-preview1, and on 4.0.7 as a check, with bundle install and a short script that loads the gem; the released eventmachine, yajl-ruby and panko_serializer failed on the preview in the same run. With both pins, thin installed and Thin::HttpParser.new succeeded on both tested Rubies. The smoke script then failed at an unrelated Thin::VERSION::STRING expression with TypeError, so this is evidence for native parser loading, not a passing complete smoke script. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.

entries.short: Play target 36: Back, edge-to-edge, tablets
entries.title: Google Play's target-36 extension ends: old back-button code, the edge-to-edge opt-out and tablet orientation locks stop working on Android 16
entries.what: Since 31 August 2026, Google Play accepts new apps and app updates only if they target Android 16 (API level 36) or higher. Developers who asked for more time got an extension to 1 November 2026. Wear OS, Android Automotive OS, Android TV and Android XR apps have lower targets, so this date is about phone and tablet apps. When an app targets 36 and runs on Android 16, predictive back is on by default, and Google says "onBackPressed is not called and KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK is not dispatched anymore". On Android 16, Google also says that at target 36 the edge-to-edge opt-out "is deprecated and disabled", and that "orientation, resizability, and aspect ratio restrictions no longer apply on displays with smallest width >= 600dp", such as tablets. In our emulator test at target 36 on Android 16, an onBackPressed() override in an Activity was never called and Back closed the screen; a KEYCODE_BACK handler in onKeyDown ran, but the screen closed anyway. In the same kind of test, a screen that used the opt-out drew its top content under the status bar, and a portrait-locked app opened in landscape on a tablet emulator. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Phone and tablet apps on Google Play can be affected if they rely on an Activity onBackPressed() override or an onKeyDown handler for KEYCODE_BACK to intercept Back, without a compatible callback or the predictive-back opt-out. Such code can handle WebView history, unsaved changes, drawers, or returning results. In our test, raising the target to 36 made Back close the screen on Android 16 despite those legacy handlers; an app already targeting 36 can encounter this before the Play deadline. We built one test app at target 35 and at target 36 and sent one Back key press to each screen, twice, on Android 16 and Android 15 emulators. At target 36 on Android 16, an onBackPressed() override in an Activity or an AppCompatActivity was never called, and the screen closed. A KEYCODE_BACK handler in onKeyDown still ran, but the screen closed anyway. At target 35, and on Android 15 at either target, every handler kept the user on the screen. Dialog.onBackPressed() and an AndroidX OnBackPressedDispatcher callback worked in every case. Cordova: with cordova-android 14.0.1 and only android-targetSdkVersion raised to 36, the backbutton event still fired, but the app closed anyway. cordova-android 15.1.0, which targets 36 by default, kept the user in the app but fired backbutton twice per press on Android 16 (once on Android 15). That is reported as cordova-android issue 2028, with a fix proposed in pull request 2029; both were open on 24 October 2026. React Native: ReactActivity overrides onBackPressed in 0.79.0 and adds an OnBackPressedCallback in 0.80.0, so apps on React Native before 0.80 are likely affected; we read the source and did not build a React Native app. Edge-to-edge: a screen is affected if its theme sets the edge-to-edge opt-out attribute to true and the screen does not apply window insets itself. In our test app on an Android 16 phone emulator, such a screen started below the 63-pixel status bar at target 35; at target 36 its content started at the top edge, under the bar. A screen that applied window insets stayed below the bar at both targets. On an Android 15 phone emulator the opt-out still worked at target 36, as Google says; that emulator failed an unrelated check in our test, so this is an observation only. Orientation: on Android 16 screens that are at least 600 dp on their shorter side, an app is affected if it locks orientation with screenOrientation in the manifest or setRequestedOrientation() in code, or limits resizing or aspect ratio. On an Android 16 tablet emulator (2560 by 1600 pixels, 800 dp on the shorter side), both kinds of portrait lock kept our app in a portrait window with bars at the sides at target 35. At target 36 the app opened in landscape, filled the screen, and its activity was recreated when we rotated the tablet; Google warns that this can lose state the app does not save. On an Android 16 phone emulator and an Android 15 tablet emulator, the lock held at both targets. Google's text also covers resizeableActivity and aspect-ratio limits; our test of those could not tell the two targets apart, so we make no claim about them. Google lists three exceptions: games that declare android:appCategory="game", screens narrower than 600 dp, and a user who chooses the app's default in the device's aspect ratio settings. To count the apps this reaches, we took the 759 open-source apps on F-Droid, with source on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg, that were updated in the past year and whose latest F-Droid build targets 35 or lower. 99 have a Google Play listing under the same package name. 23 of those have an onBackPressed() override in an Activity, no enableOnBackInvokedCallback setting, and source on the default branch that still targets 35 or lower or sets no target we could read. We read each of the 23 overrides; they go back inside a WebView, ask about unsaved changes, close a drawer or selection, return a result before closing, or keep the screen open while a transfer runs. Two more of the 99 use React Native before 0.80. On 24 October 2026 we read 98 of the same 99 apps again at their current default branch (one source link was not a repository). 9 still target 35 or lower, or set no target we could read, and set the edge-to-edge opt-out to true. 20 have the same kind of target and lock orientation or limit resizing in the manifest or in code, without the opt-out property or the game category; 6 of those 20 are games in F-Droid's catalogue. Our frozen search counted 10 and 24; reading the build files by hand showed that 5 of those apps already target 36 or 37 through a build variable. This counts code on the default branch, not the build on Google Play, and it counts a pattern, not a confirmed bug in each app. We tested on emulators only (Google APIs images for Android 16 and 15, x86_64) with a Back key press sent by adb, not the swipe gesture, and no vendor skins. With the swipe gesture there is no key event, so we expect onKeyDown handlers not to run at all; we did not test that. The edge-to-edge and orientation tests ran on 24 October 2026 on the same kinds of emulator images with software rendering, one small test layout each and two runs per case, and no foldables or desktop windows. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: Run this in your Android project. The first command lists onBackPressed and KEYCODE_BACK code, edge-to-edge opt-outs, and orientation, resizing and aspect-ratio settings. For Back, only overrides in an Activity and Back handling in onKeyDown matter, not Dialog overrides or calls. For edge-to-edge, only an opt-out set to true matters. For orientation, only the portrait and landscape values matter (such as portrait, sensorPortrait, landscape or userLandscape), not unspecified, user or fullSensor. The second command shows whether your manifest already sets enableOnBackInvokedCallback, the resizability opt-out property or android:appCategory="game". In our AGP 8.11.1 test, ./gradlew lintT36Debug reported GestureBackNavigation at Error severity; lintT35Debug did not report that issue. The default assembleT36Release build still succeeded, so run lint explicitly rather than relying on the release build to catch it. Lint does not cover the other two changes fully: in our lint run at target 36 with the same AGP version, the orientation and resizing locks got warnings only, and the edge-to-edge opt-out got no finding at all.

grep -rnE \
  --include='*.java' \
  --include='*.kt' \
  --include='*.xml' \
  -e 'onBackPressed *\(' \
  -e KEYCODE_BACK \
  -e windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement \
  -e screenOrientation \
  -e '[Rr]equestedOrientation' \
  -e resizeableActivity \
  -e 'android:m(ax|in)AspectRatio' .
grep -rn \
  --include=AndroidManifest.xml \
  -e enableOnBackInvokedCallback \
  -e COMPAT_ALLOW_RESTRICTED \
  -e appCategory .

fix.text: Stopgap: set enableOnBackInvokedCallback to "false" on the <application> tag in AndroidManifest.xml (first lines below). With it, every handler we tested kept the user on the screen again at target 36 on Android 16. Google calls this opt-out temporary, and it turns off the predictive back animations. Lasting fix: move the Back code into an AndroidX OnBackPressedDispatcher callback (second block); in an AppCompatActivity it handled Back in every build on both Android versions we tested. Google's guide says to enable the callback only while the screen needs to catch Back, for example while there are unsaved changes, and to disable it otherwise. Cordova: upgrade to cordova-android 15 rather than only raising the target, and if your backbutton handler must not run twice, follow issue 2028 for the fix. React Native, source-only recommendation: consider upgrading to 0.80 or later; ReactActivity in 0.80.0 adds the target-36 callback absent from 0.79.0. We read those two versions and did not build a React Native app or test an upgrade. We tested the opt-out and the callback on 21 October 2026, in the same emulator run (one Back key press, two repeats) as the failures above. We tested the next fixes on 24 October 2026. Edge-to-edge: there is no opt-out at target 36. Before raising the target, make each screen apply window insets itself (third block, using android.graphics.Insets and android.view.WindowInsets); in our test that kept the content below the status bar in every case. That block calls Android 11 (API 30) methods, and our test app's minSdk was 30. If your app's minSdk is below 30, use the AndroidX version instead, ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener with WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars(), as in Google's edge-to-edge guide, listed in the sources; we did not test that version. Orientation: to keep the old portrait window on tablets for now, add Google's temporary opt-out property to the application tag with the value true (its name ends in RESTRICTED_RESIZABILITY; the exact element is on Google's behavior changes page, listed in the sources); in our tablet test that restored the portrait window at target 36. Google also allows it on a single activity, and says this opt-out will not apply to apps that target API level 37. A game can instead declare android:appCategory="game", which also restored the portrait window in our test; Google lists games as an exception and gives no end date. Google's lasting fix is a layout that adapts to any orientation and size; we did not test that. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
<!-- Stopgap, in AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application
    android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="false"
    ...>

// Lasting fix, in an AppCompatActivity:
getOnBackPressedDispatcher().addCallback(this,
    new OnBackPressedCallback(true) {
        @Override
        public void handleOnBackPressed() {
            // your old onBackPressed() code
        }
    });

// Edge-to-edge (API 30+), on each root view:
root.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(
    (v, in) -> {
        Insets s = in.getInsets(
            WindowInsets.Type
                .systemBars());
        v.setPadding(s.left, s.top,
            s.right, s.bottom);
        return in;
    });

entries.short: macOS 26 runners: openssl becomes OpenSSL 4
entries.title: GitHub's macOS 26 runners switch openssl to OpenSSL 4: checks for version 3 stop matching
entries.what: From 2 November 2026, GitHub's new macOS 26 and Xcode 27 runner images run OpenSSL 4 when a workflow calls openssl without a path. The rollout is planned to finish by 8 November, "subject to compatibility validation". GitHub says: "The default openssl command will change from OpenSSL 3.x to OpenSSL 4.x on macOS 26 Intel/Arm64 and Xcode 27 Arm64 runner images." We screened 2,202 candidate openssl calls in public workflows and replayed those we could using Linux builds of OpenSSL 3.5.9, 3.6.5 and 4.0.3, as a stand-in for macOS. Within this collected sample we identified three repositories whose steps are likely to behave differently; two check for "OpenSSL 3". We did not run those repositories' workflows. On a GitHub-hosted macOS 26 runner on 22 October we ran the version check itself: with OpenSSL 4.0.3 first on the path, a check for "OpenSSL 3" left out -legacy and an old-format .p12 could not be read. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps jobs on macos-latest, macos-26 (Arm64 or Intel, any size) or the Xcode 27 image that call openssl by name. macOS 14 and 15, Ubuntu and Windows images keep their OpenSSL defaults. Our scan identified 2,202 candidate calls in 1,027 active public repositories (pushed to since 21 April 2026 and not archived). These are scan counts: at least one candidate was actually pinned to OpenSSL 3. Using the same synthetic test files under OpenSSL 3.5.9, 3.6.5 and 4.0.3, we classified 1,825 calls as unchanged, 139 as printing different text, 66 as writing different files and one as failing; 171 could not be replayed. We counted a change only when 4.0.3 differed from both 3.x versions. We read every changed call and the steps after it. Three repositories have a step that is likely to behave differently. Two decide whether to pass -legacy for an Apple .p12 file by checking that openssl version starts with "OpenSSL 3"; on OpenSSL 4 the check fails and the flag is dropped. In our test an RC2-40 .p12, the old Apple format, could not be read without -legacy on 3.5.9, 3.6.5 or 4.0.3. The third reads openssl version -e, which OpenSSL 4 no longer has ("Unknown option: -e", because engines were removed), so the library path it sets comes out empty. Other changes reach fewer scripts. Key and certificate -text dumps print hex in a new layout, with no leading 00: and 16 bytes per row; the Subject, Issuer and OID lines we checked are unchanged. Self-signed certificates made with req -x509 no longer get an Authority Key Identifier, and a certificate signed with x509 -req -CA and -extfile gets no key identifiers at all unless the file asks for them. Python 3.13 in its default strict mode then rejected such a leaf ("Missing Authority Key Identifier") when its CA had a keyUsage extension; none of the 7 repositories we found using -extfile met both conditions. We replayed the calls on OpenSSL built on Linux with Homebrew's options, as a stand-in for the macOS packages; on a macOS runner we ran only the tests this entry describes, not the collected workflows or codesign. We read only the run: lines of public workflows, not the scripts they call, composite actions, private repositories or self-hosted runners. Code search caps its results, so this is an incomplete scan, not a census of affected repositories. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: From your repository root, list the lines that check for OpenSSL 3, read openssl version -e or sign with an extension file, as below, and run the same search on any scripts your workflows call. A version check can also be written another way, such as cutting the number out of openssl version, so read the steps that handle certificates, keys or .p12 files too. In the 2,080 public workflow files we collected for affected jobs, this search found the lines in all three repositories above. To try a step on OpenSSL 4 before the switch, call $(brew --prefix openssl@4)/bin/openssl on a macos-26 job: GitHub lists OpenSSL 4 as already installed on these images, and on the macos-26 and macos-latest runners we used on 22 October it was: version 4.0.3.

fix.text: For a step that needs OpenSSL 3, call it by its Homebrew prefix (first lines below). On the macOS 26 runners we used on 22 October this printed OpenSSL 3.6.5, the same version as the default openssl there, and GitHub says it stays installed. Use it for openssl version -e too, which has no OpenSSL 4 equivalent. For a check that only needs to tell OpenSSL from LibreSSL, the openssl that comes with macOS, match '^OpenSSL [3-9]' instead of '^OpenSSL 3'. In our test that pattern matched the version line of OpenSSL 3.5.9, 3.6.5 and 4.0.3, while '^OpenSSL 3' did not match 4.0.3. Keep passing -legacy for RC2-40 .p12 files: on 4.0.3 such a file still failed to read without it and read with it, as on 3.x. If you sign certificates with x509 -req -CA and -extfile and a strict client checks them, add the two key identifier lines to that file (last lines below). On a macOS 26 runner with OpenSSL 4.0.3, a server certificate signed without them failed Python's default check ("Missing Authority Key Identifier") when the CA had keyUsage, and one signed with them passed. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
# Call OpenSSL 3 by its Homebrew prefix
OPENSSL="$(brew --prefix openssl@3)/bin/openssl"
"$OPENSSL" version
# Or accept OpenSSL 3 and later
openssl version | grep -q '^OpenSSL [3-9]'
# In the -extfile file
subjectKeyIdentifier=hash
authorityKeyIdentifier=keyid,issuer

entries.short: Chrome 157 drops the HTML-in-Canvas trial names
entries.title: Chrome 157 turns on HTML-in-Canvas without its old names: HTML textures in three.js, PlayCanvas, Babylon.js and PixiJS went blank in our tests
entries.what: Chrome 157 reached the Stable channel on 3 November 2026; Google is rolling it out over the following days and weeks. Google began sending it to a small share of Windows users on 22 October (Mac to follow) and of Android users on 23 October. Chrome 157 turns on HTML-in-Canvas, the API that draws page elements into a canvas, by default (Chrome's feature page lists it as shipping in 157), and removes the names its origin trial used: the layoutsubtree attribute, texElementImage2D (WebGL) and copyElementImageToTexture (WebGPU). In our small test scenes, the latest releases of three.js (0.186, WebGL renderer), PlayCanvas 2.23.3, Babylon.js 9.32.0 and PixiJS 8.22.0 drew an HTML texture in Chrome 156 with the feature switched on, and drew nothing in Chrome Beta 157. Only PixiJS reported an error, and it tells you to enable the API, which 157 already has on.
entries.affected: Sites and apps that draw HTML into a canvas through three.js HTMLTexture, PlayCanvas texture.setSource(element), Babylon.js HtmlTexture or PixiJS HTMLSource, or with code based on Chrome's launch post. Small pages we adapted from the post's 2D, WebGL and WebGPU examples, which use the old names, drew nothing in Chrome Beta 157 (the WebGL and WebGPU ones already failed in Chrome 156 with the feature switched on). In our three.js, PlayCanvas and PixiJS scenes, the texture drew only with the feature switched on, as the origin trial does, so the pages at risk are those using the trial today. Babylon.js was different in the configuration we tested: with its default settings, HtmlTexture drew through its SVG fallback in Chrome 156 without the trial, then drew nothing in Chrome 157. For that configuration the break reaches beyond trial sites. A larger app, for example one that marks its canvas content="drawable", may behave differently. In GitHub code search on 23 October 2026, 143 public repositories (132 owners, 77 updated in the last 30 days) had matched code files that all use the removed names and none of the new ones, after excluding forks, documentation, vendored engine files, copies of three.js source and the engine and specification repositories. That counts indexed public code only (the index can trail the latest commit), not every file in each repository, deployed sites or trial sign-ups. Executed by us on Linux, in headless Chrome for Testing with software rendering (156, Beta 157.0.8103.15, one of the builds Google began sending to Windows Stable users on 22 October, and Canary 158; the feature switched on with a command-line flag in place of a trial token; small test pages, not the engines' own examples; two fresh loads each); not independently reproduced. A real GPU, another operating system or Android may differ. Chrome's feature page lists the launch for desktop, Android and WebView; we tested desktop Linux only.
entries.check: Open the page in Chrome 157 or later and look at the canvas. If the HTML texture is missing, the page is affected; the console may show nothing. To find code that calls the removed names, search your code, including any engine files you ship with it. Using one of the four engines does not by itself mean you are affected: our results come from small test scenes, so check your own pages.
entries.checkCode:
# Names removed in Chrome 157:
grep -rni -e texElementImage2D \
  -e copyElementImageToTexture \
  -e layoutsubtree .

fix.text: Move to the API that Chrome 157 ships: mark the canvas with content="drawable" in place of layoutsubtree, mark the element drawable, and draw it inside the canvas's paint event handler with drawElementImage (2D, below), texElementSubImage2D (WebGL) or drawElementImageToTexture (WebGPU). On 23 October 2026 we ran the code below exactly as printed: it drew its element with no error in Chrome 156 with the feature switched on, in Beta 157 and in Canary 158. In 157 and 158, drawElementImage returned no transform, so the code checks for one before using it; without that check, the element still draws but the page throws an error. Our WebGL and WebGPU test pages written the new way also drew in all three. For three.js, an open pull request (#34732, not merged on 23 October) moves HTMLTexture to the new API, and with it the texture drew in Chrome 157. On 23 October no release of the four engines had a fix, and we found no issue or pull request about it for PlayCanvas, Babylon.js or PixiJS. Update, 26 October 2026: PlayCanvas merged a fix into its main branch (pull request #9824) that uses the new names and keeps the old ones as a fallback. On 26 October it was not in a published release yet (the latest on npm was 2.23.3), so watch for the next PlayCanvas release. For Babylon.js, a forum moderator reproduced the blank texture in Chrome 157.0.8103.15 and opened a fix (pull request #19052, not merged on 26 October). The reply says the update() workaround stays valid until the fix ships. We have not tested either fix. Update, 28 October 2026: Babylon.js merged its fix (pull request #19052) on 27 October. Its latest release, 9.32.1, came out earlier that day, before the merge, so no Babylon.js release has the fix yet: keep the update() workaround until one does. PlayCanvas published 2.24.0-beta.24 on 28 October. That beta uses the new names; the latest stable release is still 2.23.3, and we have not tested the beta. For PixiJS, the fix in draft pull request #12341 drew the HTML texture in Chrome 157 and 158 on our test page, with WebGL and with WebGPU. It is not merged or released, and 8.22.0 stays blank. Update, 29 October 2026: Babylon.js 9.33.0, released on 29 October, includes the fix. On our test page its HtmlTexture with default settings drew in Chrome 157 and 158, so upgrade to 9.33.0 and drop the extra update() call; with 9.33.0 that early call only logs an "HTML-in-Canvas: the native upload failed" warning. For PlayCanvas, 2.24.0-beta.24 drew the HTML texture in Chrome 157 and 158 on our test page, with WebGL2 and with WebGPU, when the canvas has content="drawable" and the element has drawable. With only the old layoutsubtree attribute, Chrome threw an InvalidStateError instead. The latest stable PlayCanvas release is still 2.23.3, which stays blank. PixiJS and three.js have no released fix yet. Update, 30 October 2026: three.js 0.187.0, released on 30 October, still uses only the old names. On our test page its HTMLTexture drew nothing in Chrome 157 and 158, with nothing in the console, and drew in Chrome 156 with the feature switched on, the same as 0.186. Upgrading three.js does not fix this yet: pull request #34732, which moves HTMLTexture to the new API, was still open on 30 October. Babylon.js 9.33.1, released on 29 October, has the same new-name code as 9.33.0; we read its build but did not run it. Update, 31 October 2026: PixiJS merged its fix (pull request #12341) on 30 October. On our test page, a PixiJS development build that includes the merged fix (8.22.0-dev.4fabfa6) drew the HTML texture in Chrome 157 and 158, with WebGL and with WebGPU, and also when the element sat one level deeper inside the canvas, with no error. On 30 October no PixiJS release had the fix yet (the latest on npm was 8.22.0), which stays blank, so watch for the next PixiJS release. For Babylon.js 9.32.0, a later run of the same test setup, on two added pages, found a workaround: calling the texture's update() yourself, once after creating it and again after each change to the element, made it draw in Chrome 157 and 158 on our small test page, through Babylon's SVG fallback rather than the new API (code and results are in our note, listed in the sources). This entry includes no workaround for PlayCanvas or PixiJS, so watch their releases. Executed by us; not independently reproduced. Update, 3 November 2026: Google promoted Chrome 157 to Stable (157.0.8103.38 for Linux, 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac), and the old names have not come back. We reran our test pages on Chrome 157.0.8103.38, the build Linux Stable serves, and every page gave the same result as in Beta 157 on 23 October: three.js 0.186.0, PlayCanvas 2.23.3 and Babylon.js 9.32.0 drew nothing and logged nothing, PixiJS 8.22.0 drew nothing and showed its error, and our test pages written with the new names drew, as did the three.js pull request (the 2D page, which has no transform check, still threw its error after drawing). On 3 November only Babylon.js had a release with the fix (9.33.0 and later). PixiJS's fix was merged but not released (the latest on npm was 8.22.0), PlayCanvas's was only in 2.24.0 beta builds (the latest release was 2.23.3), and three.js 0.187.0 still used the old names, with pull request #34732 still open. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.

entries.short: PHP 8.6 Docker images drop pecl and mbstring
entries.title: PHP 8.6 Docker images drop pecl and mbstring: pecl install and mb_ calls fail
entries.what: PHP 8.6.0 is planned for 19 November 2026. Its official Docker images have no pecl or pear command and no built-in mbstring, and every image is built thread-safe (ZTS). A Dockerfile that runs pecl install without installing the pecl command stops with "pecl: not found". PHP code that calls an mb_ function unavailable through either mbstring or a loaded polyfill stops with "Call to undefined function". The php, php:latest and php:8 tags, and currently maintained aliases such as php:fpm, php:alpine and php:8-fpm, are expected to move to 8.6 around that day: last year the 8 and latest tags moved to 8.5 on the day PHP 8.5.0 came out. Tags tied to retired distro variants may stay on older images. Tags that name a minor version, such as php:8.5-fpm, do not move. All three changes held on each 8.6.0RC4 image we tested. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Docker builds and containers on an official php image that need pecl or pear but do not install those commands, or that call mb_ functions supplied by neither mbstring nor a loaded polyfill. A build on php, php:latest, php:8 or another currently maintained alias is expected to meet this when it next pulls the moved base image, unless it is pinned by an @sha256 digest. A cached base can delay the change. A build that names 8.5 or an earlier minor meets it only when someone changes the tag to 8.6. In a code-search sample of public Dockerfiles that run pecl install on an official php image, 93% of those build stages named a minor version, such as php:8.3-fpm. The image maintainers say the change is permanent; one wrote on the pecl report: "this is intentional and this time it's for keeps." We ran 8.6.0RC4 and 8.5.12 in their cli-trixie, apache-trixie and fpm-alpine3.24 images, pinned by digest. On every 8.6 image pecl and pear were missing, pecl install apcu exited with code 127, mb_strlen() was an undefined function and PHP_ZTS was 1. On 8.5.12 pecl install apcu worked and mbstring was loaded. Composer's dependency resolution for laravel/framework 12 still succeeded on 8.6 without mbstring, because the symfony/polyfill-mbstring package stands in for it; that was a dry run, and we did not run a Laravel app. We tested release candidate 4, not the final release, and will read the final images and tags on 19 November. There is no separate zts variant for 8.6. We did not test what ZTS changes for extensions, including binary loaders such as ionCube, New Relic or Blackfire. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: Run this from your repository root. This text search lists matching PHP image references and pecl or pear calls outside vendor and node_modules. It can miss lowercase FROM instructions, continued lines, tab-separated commands, JSON-form Compose fields and image names supplied entirely by variables; review your Docker and Compose files too. php, php:latest, php:8 and currently maintained aliases such as php:fpm or php:8-fpm are expected to move to 8.6 unless an @sha256 digest follows. Retired distro variants may stay on older images. When a tag comes from an ARG, such as php:${PHP_VERSION}-fpm, read the ARG line too. If your PHP code calls mb_ functions, composer show symfony/polyfill-mbstring tells you whether your packages include the stand-in.

fix.text: To get mbstring back, install the Oniguruma headers and build it with the image's own docker-php-ext-install (first lines below). This worked on all three 8.6.0RC4 images we tested, and mb_strlen() ran afterwards. For PECL extensions, install-php-extensions supports the 8.6 release candidates from its version 2.12.5 of 28 October; an installer pinned to an earlier release still stops with "Unsupported PHP version: 8.6". On 29 October, version 2.13.1 installed gd, intl, pdo_mysql, zip, bcmath and mbstring on 8.6.0RC4 Debian and Alpine images, and the PECL extensions mongodb, uuid, xhprof and event. The image has no pecl, so the installer sets up PEAR itself. apcu 5.1.28 and phpredis 6.3.0, their latest releases, still fail to compile on 8.6, with the installer and with PIE 1.5.3: both projects have merged fixes for 8.6 but, as of 30 October, have not released them. If you need apcu, phpredis or another extension whose latest release does not build on 8.6, keep a tag that names 8.5 (last line below). On 8.5.12, pecl install apcu still worked. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
# Debian images: build mbstring
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y libonig-dev \
 && docker-php-ext-install mbstring
# Alpine images
RUN apk add --no-cache oniguruma-dev \
 && docker-php-ext-install mbstring
# If you need apcu or phpredis
FROM php:8.5-fpm
fix.label: The tested install-php-extensions step, with the apcu and phpredis errors

entries.short: node:lts becomes Node 26: no Yarn, no Corepack
entries.time: tag move expected that day or shortly after; not announced
entries.title: node:lts becomes Node 26: yarn and corepack are no longer in the image
entries.what: Node.js 26 becomes the long-term support (LTS) release on 28 October 2026. The official Docker image's lts tags are expected to move from Node 24 to Node 26 that day or shortly after: they moved to Node 24 on the same day last year, and our run of the image's own tag generator, dated 28 October, moved node:lts, node:lts-slim and node:lts-alpine. The maintainers have not announced a time. Node 26 images include neither Yarn v1 nor Corepack, so a build that runs yarn or corepack without installing it first will fail. The node:lts and node:lts-slim tags also move from Debian 12 (bookworm) to Debian 13 (trixie), whose apt has no apt-key command. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: The missing commands come from the image maintainers' notes and the Node.js 25.0.0 changelog, and we checked them on a Node 26.11.1 slim image: it has no yarn, corepack or apt-key. Affected are Dockerfile stages, Compose services and CI jobs whose image is a node:lts tag without an @sha256 digest. Our run of the tag generator moves every one of these tags to Node 26, including node:lts-alpine and node:lts-bookworm (only the name tag node:lts-krypton stays on Node 24), so a stage or job that runs yarn or corepack without first getting it breaks. Only node:lts and node:lts-slim also move to Debian 13, so apt-key breaks on those two tags only. A yarn, corepack or apt-key command in a RUN step fails at the first build after the tag moves, not on the day itself; a cached base image can delay that. A yarn command that appears only in CMD or ENTRYPOINT does not stop the build: the new container fails when it starts. Tags that name a major version, such as node:24-slim, do not move. We searched GitHub code for Dockerfiles containing FROM node:lts and read a 5% sample, spread evenly across file sizes, on default branches. In that sample, 44 repositories that were not forks or archived and had been pushed to since 25 April 2026 have a stage like this: 29 run corepack, 17 run yarn during the build, 5 start the app with yarn and 2 use apt-key (some do more than one). Scaled up from the 5% sample, that is about 880 repositories. We read all 44: three are doubtful (a blog snippet, a backup file and a build that runs yarn only if npm fails), but the rule we fixed before the run counts them. Separately, among .gitlab-ci.yml files on GitHub that use a node:lts image, 23 such repositories have a yarn line and no yarn install anywhere in the file. The search misses FROM lines with --platform or a registry name, and reading a file cannot tell whether it is still built. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: Run this from your repository root. This text search lists lines that name a node:lts image, and lines that name yarn, corepack or apt-key, in Dockerfiles and YAML files outside node_modules. For each build stage or CI job whose image is a node:lts tag without an @sha256 digest, look at its yarn and corepack lines: on Node 26 each one fails unless the stage gets the tool first, for example with npm install --global, a system package or a COPY from another image. apt-key fails only on node:lts and node:lts-slim. A yarn command only in CMD or ENTRYPOINT fails when the container starts, not during the build. The search also lists lines that are fine, such as copies of yarn.lock. It misses images named through a variable, such as node:${NODE_TAG}; read your ARG lines too. On the Dockerfiles in our sample, it listed every file we counted.

fix.text: Pin the Node major you build on today. node:24, node:24-slim and node:24-alpine stay on Node 24, which Node.js supports until 30 April 2028, and node:24 and node:24-slim stay on Debian 12. We ran Node 24.22 images (Debian 12 and Alpine) with no network: yarn 1.22.22 and corepack 0.36.0 were there, and yarn install worked offline on an empty project. When you move to Node 26, add Yarn or Corepack yourself, following the image maintainers' notes and Corepack's own instructions, and replace apt-key as your third-party repository describes for Debian 13. Install lines for Yarn, Corepack and pnpm that passed install-and-version checks on Node 24 and 26 images are in the guide below.
fix.code:
# Before
FROM node:lts-slim
# After: stay on Node 24
FROM node:24-slim
fix.label: Install lines for Yarn, Corepack and pnpm, checked on Node 24 and 26

entries.short: DuckDB 1.4 LTS ends; 2.0 drops rel.fetchone()
entries.title: DuckDB 1.4 LTS support ends: DuckDB 2.0 drops fetchone() on relations and rejects x -> lambdas
entries.what: DuckDB 1.4, the long-term support (LTS) release, reaches end of life on 17 November 2026; DuckDB 1.5 is supported until March 2027. DuckDB 2.0.0 came out on 21 October 2026, and on Python 3.11 and newer, pip install duckdb now installs it. In 2.0, a relation (what duckdb.sql(), con.sql() and duckdb.query() return) no longer has fetchone(), fetchmany() or execute(), and the result of con.execute() no longer has fetch_arrow_table(), arrow() or pl(); each call raises AttributeError. In our runs of 1.4.5, 1.5.5 and 1.5.6, fetchone() and fetchmany() on a relation gave no deprecation warning first. In SQL, a lambda written with a single arrow, such as list_transform(l, x -> x + 1), fails with a Binder Error. A database moved the way DuckDB's migration guide shows, with EXPORT DATABASE on 1.x and IMPORT DATABASE on 2.0, does not import if a view or macro uses such a lambda: the import stops with that error, and in our tests no tables were created. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Nothing stops working on 17 November itself: DuckDB 1.4 stops getting fixes, and code that stays on 1.4 or moves to 1.5 works as before. The changes hit code that runs on 2.0, which includes any project that installs duckdb without an upper version limit on Python 3.11 or newer; on Python 3.10, pip still installs 1.5.6. One more 2.0 change catches the obvious replacement: a con.execute() result that has not been read to its end makes the next con.sql(), duckdb.sql() or duckdb.query() on the same connection fail with a ResourceInUseException, even after fetchone() on a one-row query. DuckDB's Python migration guide describes this; 1.5.6 does not do it. Libraries are affected too. Of the 72 packages among the 15,000 most downloaded from PyPI that list duckdb as a dependency, 26 allow only versions below 2. Six others call a removed method in their latest release as of 22 October: dlt 1.31.0 (DuckLake loads fail, as reported in its issue tracker), ibis-framework 12.0.0 (list_tables() on the DuckDB backend), narwhals 2.27.1 (time-zone-aware DuckDB columns), sqlglot 30.24.0 (DuckDB SQL it generates can contain x -> lambdas), and marimo 0.25.2 and marimo-base 0.25.2 (default database and schema lookups return None without an error). ibis, narwhals and sqlglot have fixes on their main branches that are not yet released; dlt has an open issue; we found no report for marimo. We found these calls by reading each package's source and did not run the packages on 2.0; a source scan finds only direct calls, so there may be more. In a capped sample of public GitHub code, 22 active repositories of user code use single-arrow lambdas; we separated them from copies of DuckDB itself and test data after the search. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: Run the text search below from your repository root. It lists Python lines that call fetchone() or fetchmany() at the end of a chain, call execute() on a relation, or call fetch_arrow_table(), arrow() or pl(). For each line, see whether the object is a DuckDB relation, a DuckDB execute() result that is not read to its end, or something else. On the latest releases of the 72 packages it listed 34 of the 35 removed calls we found by reading their source; it missed one where the relation was kept in a variable and fetched on a later line. It also lists many lines that are fine, such as fetchone() in other database libraries. For SQL, DuckDB 1.4 and 1.5 can show the 2.0 lambda error today: run the SET statement at the start of a session, then your queries, views and macros. In our runs on 1.4.5, 1.5.5 and 1.5.6, every single-arrow lambda then failed with the same Binder Error as on 2.0, including one in a view created earlier, while lambda x: lambdas and JSON's -> operator still worked.
entries.checkCode:
# Python (text search):
grep -rnE --include='*.py' \
  -e '\)\.fetch(one|many)\(' \
  -e '(sql|query)\(.*\)\.execute\(' \
  -e 'fetch_arrow_table\(' \
  -e '\.(arrow|pl)\(\)' .
-- SQL, on DuckDB 1.4 or 1.5:
SET lambda_syntax=
  'disable_single_arrow';

fix.text: Read results in a way that works on 1.5 and 2.0 and leaves nothing open: take the first row from con.sql(query).limit(1).fetchall(), read an execute() result with fetchmany() until it returns an empty list, and get Arrow tables from con.sql(query).to_arrow_table(). con.execute(query).fetchone() also works on 2.0, but call con.complete() (2.0 only) before the next con.sql() on that connection. Write SQL lambdas as lambda x: x + 1, which works on 1.4, 1.5 and 2.0; on 2.0, SET lambda_syntax='enable_single_arrow' brings the arrow form back for the session until DuckDB 2.1 removes the setting. To move a database file to 2.0, run that SET before IMPORT DATABASE, or copy the file with COPY FROM DATABASE. A 1.x file opened directly in 2.0 kept its arrow-lambda views working when it was written at the default storage version, but they failed when it was written with STORAGE_VERSION 'v1.3.0' or later, until the same SET was run. Until the libraries you use release fixes, duckdb<2 keeps you on 1.5; it installs 1.5.6 today. We ran each of these on 2.0.0 and the Python lines on 1.5.6 too, each followed by another query on the same connection.
fix.code:
# Python, before (fails on 2.0):
row = con.sql(query).fetchone()
table = con.execute(query).fetch_arrow_table()
# after (1.5 and 2.0):
rows = con.sql(query).limit(1).fetchall()
row = rows[0] if rows else None
table = con.sql(query).to_arrow_table()
-- SQL, before (fails on 2.0):
SELECT list_transform(l, x -> x + 1) FROM t;
-- after (1.4, 1.5 and 2.0):
SELECT list_transform(l, lambda x: x + 1) FROM t;
-- moving an EXPORT DATABASE folder to 2.0:
SET lambda_syntax='enable_single_arrow';
IMPORT DATABASE 'export_dir';
# or stay on 1.5 for now:
pip install 'duckdb<2'
