entries.short: Quad9 leaves France; AdGuard Home default fails
entries.title: Quad9 leaves France: a default AdGuard Home install stops resolving names there
entries.what: Quad9, the public DNS resolver at 9.9.9.9, announced on 22 October 2026 that it will withdraw its services from France as of Tuesday 24 November, because of a French court order. It has not said how: a user in France might get no answer, a refused connection or a refusal message. AdGuard Home's install wizard (v0.107.79; v0.107.80 of 3 November keeps the same defaults in its source) sets Quad9 as the only upstream DNS server and the only bootstrap DNS server, with no fallback. We ran that default configuration with Quad9 made unreachable in four ways (packets dropped, connections rejected, REFUSED answers, and HTTP 451 from its DNS-over-HTTPS address). From a fresh start, 0 of 20 names resolved in every case, each with SERVFAIL, in two runs. On a running server, names already in the cache kept working and new names failed. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: People in France who run AdGuard Home with the DNS settings its install wizard chose, and every device that uses it as its DNS server. A working system resolver on the same machine does not help, because AdGuard Home does not use it for these lookups. Two other setups still depend on Quad9. An upstream written as a hostname, such as https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query, with the default bootstrap servers kept working while it ran but resolved 0 of 20 names after a restart. Adding a fallback DNS server helps only partly: it rescued a fresh start, but on a running server new names still failed when Quad9 dropped packets (no answer within 5 seconds) or answered REFUSED (AdGuard Home passed the refusal on to clients). Any other resolver or device in France that sends its queries to Quad9 (9.9.9.9, 149.112.112.112 or dns.quad9.net) loses that service too; we tested only AdGuard Home. Of 685 public AdGuardHome.yaml files we read on GitHub, 120 (18%) use Quad9 as their only upstream, 80 of them with the wizard's settings unchanged; these are published configs, not a count of installs, and not specific to France. Router, NAS and add-on builds that include AdGuard Home may ship other defaults; we did not test them.
entries.check: Open Settings, then DNS settings (in French: Paramètres, then Paramètres DNS), and read the Upstream DNS servers and Bootstrap DNS servers lists. You are affected if every general upstream server (a line without [/domain/] in front) is Quad9 (9.9.9.x, 149.112.112.x, 2620:fe:: addresses or a quad9.net name), or if your upstream servers are written as hostnames and every bootstrap server is a Quad9 address. If you manage the file instead, the command below prints the same lists from AdGuardHome.yaml (in the official Docker image it is in /opt/adguardhome/conf); if upstream_dns_file is set, the upstream list is in that file.

fix.text: Before 24 November, in Settings, then DNS settings (Paramètres, then Paramètres DNS), replace the Quad9 entry under Upstream DNS servers (Serveurs DNS upstream) with a resolver you trust that is not Quad9, written as an IP address (for example 1.1.1.1, or the DNS-over-HTTPS form below), and click Apply (Appliquer). If you want to keep an upstream written as a hostname, also set Bootstrap DNS servers (Serveurs DNS d'amorçage) to non-Quad9 IP addresses. In our runs, both setups resolved every name in all four withdrawal cases, from a fresh start and on a running server. We also made each change, including a plain 1.1.1.1, on a running default install through the API that the settings page uses, then dropped or rejected Quad9 traffic and restarted AdGuard Home: new names resolved before and after the restart, and the change was saved. Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 was our test stand-in; any non-Quad9 resolver is the same change. A fallback DNS server alone is not enough. If you edit AdGuardHome.yaml instead, the keys are upstream_dns and bootstrap_dns; restart AdGuard Home afterwards.
fix.code:
# Upstream DNS servers, default:
https://dns10.quad9.net/dns-query
# replace with a non-Quad9 IP:
https://1.1.1.1/dns-query
# or, for a hostname upstream, set
# Bootstrap DNS servers to IPs:
1.1.1.1
1.0.0.1

entries.short: Azure ubuntu-latest → 26.04: /home/vsts is gone
entries.time: the end of a rollout that began on 19 October; a project can switch on any day before
entries.title: Azure Pipelines moves ubuntu-latest to Ubuntu 26.04: steps that hard-code /home/vsts fail
entries.what: Microsoft moves the ubuntu-latest image in Azure Pipelines from Ubuntu 24.04 to 26.04 over several weeks, starting 19 October and finishing by 19 November 2026. YAML pipelines that set no pool get the same image. On 26.04 the agent runs as a different user: its home folder and the pipeline workspace move from /home/vsts to /home/runner, and /home/vsts does not exist. Microsoft's announcement does not mention this; a user reported it on 22 October. In public 26.04 jobs we read in two Azure DevOps organizations on 22 and 23 October, the checkout was under /home/runner/work; a 24.04 job in the same build as one of them checked out under /home/vsts/work. We ran common uses of the old path in a copy of the new layout, twice each. These failed: cd, ls or writing a file under /home/vsts/work, running a tool by its full /home/vsts/.local/bin path, mkdir -p under /home/vsts, and a uv or npm cache set to a folder there. Adding /home/vsts/.local/bin to PATH is harmless, because the 26.04 image's PATH already has /home/runner/.local/bin; a pip cache there only makes pip warn and install without its cache. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Azure DevOps YAML pipelines on Microsoft-hosted ubuntu-latest, or with no pool set, whose scripts, variables or task inputs write a /home/vsts/... path. Jobs pinned to ubuntu-24.04 or ubuntu-22.04, self-hosted agents and steps inside container jobs are not affected by this switch. GitHub Actions is not affected: its runners already use /home/runner. With default settings, a later command that succeeds can hide an earlier failed one: the step passes and the file, folder or cache is simply missing. With set -e, an explicit error check or a task setting such as failOnStderr, the step can fail at that line instead. In public GitHub code, we read 53 files in 43 repositories that mention /home/vsts and had an Azure Pipelines check on their latest default-branch commit, committed since 23 April 2026. We flagged 20 of them, from 12 owners (9 from one owner), as potentially affected: in 15, the flagged line matches a use we ran in a copy of the new layout; in 5, it depends on how a third-party tool handles the missing folder, which we did not test. One is mne-python, where the uv cache setting stops its dependency install. This is the public code we read, not a count of pipelines that will fail; private pipelines were not examined. We did not test Cache@2 paths, Docker volume paths or third-party tasks that take a /home/vsts path.
entries.check: From your repository root, search pipeline files and scripts for the old path, as below. A match alone does not mean a break. For each match in a job on ubuntu-latest or with no pool, look for the uses that failed in our runs: cd, ls or writing a file under /home/vsts/work, running a tool by its full /home/vsts path, mkdir -p there, or a uv or npm cache there. A PATH entry or a pip cache there does not stop the job. Variables set in the Azure DevOps web interface or in variable groups are not in the files, so look there too. Once a job's checkout log shows /home/runner/work, the switch has happened for that pipeline.

fix.text: In script and bash lines, replace /home/vsts with $HOME. In YAML values such as variables:, env: and task inputs, no shell expands $HOME, so use the agent's own variables there, as below, and put a cache in a folder under $(Pipeline.Workspace). Or pin vmImage: ubuntu-24.04 until you have made the change. In our runs, every failing use worked with $HOME in both the old and the new layout. A uv or npm cache set in an environment variable to a folder under the workspace worked in both; set to $HOME/.cache/uv, uv made a folder literally named $HOME inside the checkout. In a public 26.04 job, $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory) became /home/runner/work/1/a. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
# in script: and bash: lines
$HOME/.local/bin/mytool
# in variables:, env:, inputs
# /home/vsts/work/1/s becomes
$(Build.SourcesDirectory)
# /home/vsts/work/1
$(Pipeline.Workspace)
# /home/vsts/work/_temp
$(Agent.TempDirectory)
# /home/vsts/work/1/a
$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)
# a cache, e.g. UV_CACHE_DIR:
$(Pipeline.Workspace)/.uv
# or, until you have changed it
pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-24.04

entries.short: Langfuse Cloud turns off its deprecated APIs
entries.time: 00:00 UTC, the time in the API's Sunset header
entries.title: Langfuse Cloud stops serving its deprecated APIs: old trace, session and metrics reads and trace ingestion fail
entries.what: 16 November 2026 is Langfuse Cloud's cutover to Langfuse v4. From then, Cloud stops serving the public API endpoints that its migration guide lists as deprecated. Reads: GET /api/public/traces, /observations and /sessions (and each one's /{id} form), /metrics and /metrics/daily, /scores and /v2/scores, and the dataset-run endpoints (/datasets/{name}/runs and /dataset-run-items). Writes: POST /dataset-run-items, trace and observation events sent to POST /api/public/ingestion, and the older POST /traces, /spans, /generations and /events (and PATCH /spans and /generations). SDK methods that call these endpoints fail with them, such as client.api.trace.list() in Python SDK v4 and fetchTraces() in JS/TS SDK v5. On 23 October a request to GET /api/public/traces returned a Sunset header of 16 November 2026, 00:00 UTC. Score writes keep working: POST /api/public/scores, and score-create events that older SDKs send to /ingestion. This date is for Langfuse Cloud only. Self-hosted Langfuse has no forced cutover date, and Langfuse says v3 gets security patches through January 2027.
entries.affected: Code that calls Langfuse Cloud through one of these endpoints or methods: scripts and dashboards that read traces, sessions or daily metrics, exporters that copy traces elsewhere, and tools, proxies or SDKs in other languages that send traces to /ingestion rather than through OpenTelemetry. Langfuse emails the owners and admins of each Cloud project a summary of the actions that project needs, and its migration status page (cloud.langfuse.com/v4-migration) lists the SDK, API, evaluator and integration actions it detected; if you run a Cloud project, start there. This date is for code that email may not reach: libraries and tools that wrap Langfuse for their own users, public example code that others copy, and self-hosted servers whose owners are choosing when to upgrade. On 23 October we searched public GitHub code for six endpoint paths that the removal touches. 797 repositories matched; 574 of them are not forks, not archived and were pushed to since 1 July. We read a random sample of 10 of the 574. 6 call a removed endpoint: 3 send trace or generation events to /ingestion, and 3 read traces or observations, 2 of them using trace timestamps. The other 4 were documentation, notes or a copy of Langfuse's own server. Within these 574 repositories, the sample gives an estimate of about 340 with a deprecated call site (95% Wilson confidence interval: about 180–480; sample size 10). This is not a census or a lower bound on affected Langfuse Cloud repositories. We retrieved at most 300 files per endpoint search and excluded forks and archived repositories. The search misses private code, paths built at run time, and SDK calls that do not spell out the endpoint path. We did not establish how many of these repositories use Langfuse Cloud rather than self-hosted servers. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.check: If you run a Langfuse Cloud project, open its migration status page first: it lists what Langfuse detected for that project. To check code, run the text search below from your repository root. It lists lines that name a removed endpoint path or call an SDK method that Langfuse's migration guide maps to a replacement. A hit means read the line, not that it breaks: POST /api/public/scores and /ingestion calls that carry only score events match too and keep working, and client.api.scores.get_many() is affected only on Python SDK v4 (getMany() only on JS/TS SDK v5). The search does not see SDK versions, so also look up langfuse in your lock files: Langfuse asks Cloud projects that send traces with its SDKs to move to Python SDK 4.7.0 or later or JS/TS SDK 5.4.0 or later before 16 November. On 23 October the search found every call in the 6 sampled repositories that call a removed endpoint, all 36 deprecated calls we copied from Langfuse's migration guide, and none of 24 replacement calls and look-alikes.

fix.text: Langfuse's migration guide maps each removed endpoint and SDK method to its replacement; we have not run them against Langfuse. Trace, observation and session reads move to Observations API v2 (GET /api/public/v2/observations), which returns one row per observation, not trace objects. Ask for fields=core,basic,trace_context to get the trace name, tags and release on each row, and group rows by traceId to rebuild a trace; a trace's old name filter becomes a filter on the traceName column. Metrics API v2 has no traces view. For trace counts, filter on isRootObservation = true; for cost totals grouped by trace attributes, aggregate observation costs. Its latency metrics describe observations. For trace duration or raw per-trace data, use Observations API v2 and group rows by traceId. Score reads move to GET /api/public/v3/scores, and dataset runs become experiments (GET /api/public/experiments and /experiment-items). To send traces, use Python SDK 4.7.0 or later, JS/TS SDK 5.4.0 or later, or OpenTelemetry to /api/public/otel/v1/traces with the header x-langfuse-ingestion-version: 4. Python SDK v5 and JS/TS SDK v6 drop the old methods; they need Langfuse Cloud or self-hosted Langfuse 4.59.0 or later. Dataset-backed experiment runners in Python SDK v4 and JS/TS SDK v5 still call POST /dataset-run-items themselves; Langfuse's advice there is to keep the SDK updated.
fix.code:
# before (fails on Langfuse Cloud from 16 Nov)
curl -G -u "$PK:$SK" "$HOST/api/public/traces"
# after: one row per observation; group by traceId
curl -G -u "$PK:$SK" "$HOST/api/public/v2/observations" \
  --data-urlencode "fields=core,basic,trace_context" \
  --data-urlencode "fromStartTime=2026-11-01T00:00:00Z" \
  --data-urlencode "toStartTime=2026-11-08T00:00:00Z"
# Python SDK v4: client.api.trace.list(...) becomes
# client.api.observations.get_many(
#     from_start_time=..., to_start_time=...)
fix.label: Langfuse's migration guide: every removed endpoint and SDK method with its replacement

entries.short: Bioconductor 3.24: some packages fail to install
entries.title: Bioconductor 3.24: fresh R 4.6 installs fail for packages missing from it, including some the removal list does not name
entries.what: Bioconductor plans to release version 3.24, for R 4.6, on Wednesday 25 November 2026. From then, BiocManager::install() in an R 4.6 library that is not already on a Bioconductor version (a new laptop, a CI job, a Docker build, a course image) installs from 3.24, and a package that is not in 3.24 fails with "package 'X' is not available for Bioconductor version '3.24'". Libraries already on 3.23 keep working until someone upgrades them. Bioconductor's removed-packages page lists 54 packages as deprecated in 3.23 and to be removed in 3.24. On 25 October we compared that list with the source package indexes that BiocManager reads: 28 of the 54 were already missing from 3.23, and 47 packages that are in 3.23 were missing from the 3.24 index without being on the list. Most of the 47 are rarely downloaded. The exceptions are decoupleR and two packages that depend on it, dorothea and progeny. decoupleR fails R CMD check on all three of Bioconductor's 3.24 builders, its last change on Bioconductor's development branch was on 28 April 2026, and in December 2025 its maintainers set its GitHub repository to ask people to open issues in the Python decoupler repository instead, saying the R repository is no longer maintained. Bioconductor's deadline for packages to pass build and check is 20 November. These packages can still be fixed and added before the release; this entry says what was missing on 25 October, not what Bioconductor will remove. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: R 4.6 users who install Bioconductor packages from source into a library that is not already on 3.23 after 25 November: Linux machines, CI jobs, Docker builds, and course or core-facility images that run BiocManager::install() without a version. In Bioconductor's download statistics for January to July 2026, decoupleR averaged about 3,250 distinct IP addresses a month, dorothea about 2,000 and progeny about 1,400; these include mirrors, CI and bots, so they are not counts of people. On Windows and macOS, 14 of the 47 still had an older binary package that may install; we did not test those platforms. Installs that ask for version = "3.23" and existing 3.23 libraries are not affected until they are upgraded. R 4.5 stays on Bioconductor 3.22. This says nothing about the scientific quality of any package.
entries.check: Run the lines below in R 4.6, in the library you want to check, with BiocManager installed. They list the Bioconductor packages installed there that are missing from the 3.24 index; until 25 November that is Bioconductor's development version. An empty result means nothing installed is missing today. Packages can still be added or dropped before the release, so run it again after 20 November. On 25 October, in a 3.23 library with BiocGenerics and decoupleR installed, it printed only decoupleR. It finds Bioconductor packages by the git_url field that Bioconductor's builds add. It does not check dependencies: on 25 October, 12 packages were in the 3.24 index but could not be installed because a package they need was missing. We ran it on Linux only, with BiocManager 1.30.27; on Windows and macOS it reads the binary package index, which we did not test.
entries.checkCode:
ip <- installed.packages(fields = "git_url")
bioc <- rownames(ip)[grepl("git.bioconductor.org",
  ip[, "git_url"], fixed = TRUE)]
nxt <- rownames(available.packages(repos =
  BiocManager::repositories(version = "3.24")))
sort(setdiff(bioc, nxt))

fix.code:
BiocManager::install(version = "3.23",
  ask = FALSE)
BiocManager::install("decoupleR",
  version = "3.23", ask = FALSE, update = FALSE)
fix.text: To keep a package that is missing from 3.24, move the library to 3.23 first, then install the package. The one-line pin, BiocManager::install("decoupleR", version = "3.23"), stops by design with "To use Bioconductor version '3.23', first downgrade … packages with BiocManager::install(version = '3.23')" and installs nothing. The two commands below installed decoupleR and its 30 dependencies into a new library, and later install() calls in that library stayed on 3.23. We ran them on Linux in R 4.6.1 with BiocManager 1.30.27, using a copy of Bioconductor's version file edited so that 3.24 is the release, because 3.24 is not out yet. Bioconductor stops building 3.23 on 9 November, so this keeps an analysis installing; it does not bring later fixes. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.

entries.short: ArcGIS: 1,121 Living Atlas items retire
entries.title: ArcGIS Online: Esri retires 1,121 Living Atlas items in December 2026, and maps that still use them lose those layers
entries.what: Esri tags the ArcGIS Living Atlas items it will retire this December with "retiring-2026-12". On 26 October 2026 a public ArcGIS Online search for that tag returned 1,143 items; 1,121 of them are Esri's own items marked Deprecated, and the other 22 are other users' items that carry the tag without a notice. 620 of Esri's 1,121 belong to its demographics account. Others include USA Parks, Active Wildfires in Canada, National Water Model forecasts, World Time Zones and HYCOM ocean forecasts. 1,120 of the 1,121 descriptions carry a retirement notice naming December 2026 (1,119 in English and one in Spanish); the remaining item says Fall 2026. For example "This item is in mature support as of October 2024 and will retire in December 2026." The notices give the month, not a day. Esri announced its previous batch as unavailable after 10 December 2025. In 691 of the 1,121 notices Esri says "A replacement item has not been identified." Esri's help says items retired from ArcGIS Online "will no longer work in existing maps and apps". Earlier retirements show what that looks like. The old USA_Counties feature service that Esri ran answers "Invalid URL" today while its replacement works, and on 26 October 10 of the 2,814 most-viewed public web maps from accounts whose names do not start with "Esri" still used it. Those maps still open, without the county layer. Executed by us on 26 October; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Owners of ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise maps, apps and dashboards that use one of these items, and anyone who embeds or links to such a map. On 26 October, 5 of the 2,814 most-viewed public web maps from accounts whose names do not start with "Esri" (0.18%) used a retiring item; 3 of the 5 are public wildfire maps that use USA Parks. We can only see public maps. Most retiring items are demographic layers, which we expect are used mainly in maps inside organisations, so public maps probably understate how many maps are affected.
entries.check: Each retiring item's page in ArcGIS Online shows a Deprecated badge and Esri's retirement notice, also to visitors who are not signed in. For a public web map, the Python lines below list every layer whose item is tagged retiring-2026-12 and marked Deprecated. They need Python 3 and no packages or sign-in. Give the map's item ID, the 32-character id= value in its address. They read only layers that the map adds by item ID, not layers added by URL alone. For an app or dashboard, give the web map inside it. A private map, or an item that is not a web map, stops with "not a public web map". On 26 October it printed USA Parks for a public wildfire map that we knew used it, and printed nothing for a map with no retiring layers. Run it before December: once Esri removes a retired item, these lines no longer list it.
entries.checkCode:
import json, re, sys, urllib.request
A = "https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest"
A += "/content/items/"
def get(path):
    u = A + path + "?f=json"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(u) as r:
        return json.load(r)
mid = sys.argv[1]
if get(mid).get("type") != "Web Map":
    sys.exit("not a public web map: " + mid)
m = json.dumps(get(mid + "/data"))
ids = re.findall(r'"itemId": "(\w{32})"', m)
for i in sorted(set(ids)):
    it = get(i)
    if ("retiring-2026-12" in it.get("tags", [])
            and it.get("contentStatus") == "deprecated"):
        print("RETIRING", i, it["title"])

fix.text: Where the item's notice says a new version is available, Esri recommends updating your maps and apps to use it; look for it from the old item's page. After switching, check that the layer's pop-ups and symbols still work, because we did not compare old and new items. Where the notice says no replacement has been identified (691 items), remove the layer or find other data before December. We did not test any replacement.

entries.short: US clocks go back: Celery beat pauses
entries.title: US clocks go back: Celery beat interval tasks stop for an hour, and a beat started inside it can send crontabs in a loop
entries.what: Daylight saving time ends in most of the US at 02:00 local time on 1 November 2026, so 01:00 to 01:59 happens twice.
entries.affected: Celery beat 5.6.3, the current stable release, and 5.5.3 with beat's timezone set to America/New_York. In our controlled-clock test of the real beat scheduler, interval schedules stopped for the repeated hour: an every-minute task missed 60 runs from 06:00 to 06:59 UTC, an every-5-minute task missed 12 and an hourly task missed one. The enable_utc setting made no difference. Crontab schedules every 15 minutes or on the hour skipped the repeated hour's times in every version we tested, 5.7.0rc1 included. Daily crontab jobs at 01:30 and 02:00 ran once; nothing ran twice. Other US time zones, a beat restart inside the hour, django-celery-beat's database scheduler, and delivery through a broker to workers were not tested. Update, 2 November: a production report on Celery 5.6.2 in America/Los_Angeles describes beat sending every crontab entry in a loop from 01:00 to 02:00 PST, 149,010 messages in about 26 minutes; deleting the schedule file and restarting beat inside the hour started the loop again. We ran the report's test, which checks the schedule every 10 seconds, from 01:20 PST for 40 minutes: an every-6-minute crontab came due 204 times and an every-15-minute crontab 150 times instead of 6 and 2, on 5.5.3, 5.6.3, 5.7.0rc1 and Celery's main branch of 2 November alike. Those counts depend on the 10-second step. In Celery's own scheduler on a simulated clock, a beat started at 01:20 PST on 5.6.3, 5.7.0rc1 or main stopped waiting between checks, so a real beat sends as fast as it can loop. A daily crontab at 01:30 also looped until 01:30 PST passed; an hourly crontab did not. A beat already running before the change did not loop in our tests; the report does not say how its first loop began.
entries.check: Find beat's timezone in your Celery configuration (timezone, or CELERY_TIMEZONE in Django settings). If it is a US zone, entries in the beat schedule given as a number of seconds, a timedelta or schedule() are interval tasks; entries given as crontab() are crontabs.

fix.text: If a one-hour pause at 1 a.m. is acceptable, no change is needed. To keep interval tasks running, 5.7.0rc1 ran every interval task in our test; it is a release candidate, published on 18 October with Celery's fix (pull request #10769), so try it outside production first. On 5.6.3, a UTC beat timezone also ran every interval task, but it moves every crontab entry to UTC times, so use it only where every entry is an interval. Neither change stops crontabs every 15 minutes or on the hour from skipping the repeated hour's times. Executed by us; not independently reproduced. 5.7.0rc1 does not stop the loop in the test above. Celery's open pull request #10608, planned for 5.8.0, did in our run of the same test: 6 and 2 sends in 40 minutes, the correct counts.
fix.code:
pip install \
  'celery==5.7.0rc1'

entries.short: US clocks go back: sidekiq-cron jobs run twice
entries.title: US clocks go back: sidekiq-cron daily jobs set between 01:00 and 01:59 run twice
entries.what: Daylight saving time ends in most of the US at 02:00 local time on 1 November 2026, so 01:00 to 01:59 happens twice.
entries.affected: sidekiq-cron 2.4.0, the current release, with Sidekiq 8.1.7 and fugit 1.14.0. In our controlled-clock test of the real poller and Redis, a daily job at 01:30 America/New_York was enqueued at 05:30 and again at 06:30 UTC, whether the process ran in UTC or New York time; a daily 01:00 job did the same. A daily 01:15 line with no time zone ran twice in each setup where it followed New York time: with TZ=America/New_York, in a Rails app set to Eastern time, or on a server set to New York time. Hourly and every-30-minute jobs ran on time, and daily jobs at 02:30 and 09:00 ran once. Earlier versions, other US time zones, several Sidekiq processes and Sidekiq Enterprise periodic jobs were not tested.
entries.check: Search your schedule (config/schedule.yml by default, or Sidekiq::Cron::Job.create calls) for cron lines whose hour is 1. A line with no time zone follows the TZ variable of the Sidekiq process if it is set; treat the line as affected if that is a US zone. Without TZ, treat it as affected if the server's time zone or, in a Rails app, config.time_zone is a US zone. The search below finds standard, natural-language ("every day at 1:30") and unquoted lines, hour ranges and hour lists. It also shows lines that run on the 1st of the month; skip those.

fix.text: Move the job out of 01:00 to 01:59 local time, for example to 02:30. That ran once, at 02:30 in the zone the line follows, in every setup we tested. Or write its cron line in UTC, but only if the Sidekiq process has the TZ variable set. With TZ set, 30 6 * * * UTC ran once at 06:30 UTC, which is 01:30 in New York from 1 November and 02:30 in summer. On a server set to New York time with TZ not set, the same line ran at 06:30 New York time. We reported the cause, with a fix sketch, to fugit's maintainers. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
fix.code:
my_job:
  cron: "30 2 * * *"
  class: "MyJob"

entries.short: IRS FIRE stops taking 1099 e-files
entries.title: IRS closes FIRE: Publication 1220 files for Forms 1099 can no longer be e-filed
entries.what: The IRS's FIRE system takes its last information returns at 3 p.m. Eastern time on 19 November 2026 (20:00 UTC). FIRE takes Forms 1097, 1098, 1099, 3921, 3922, 5498 and W-2G as fixed-width files laid out by IRS Publication 1220, and the IRS says Publication 1220 will be made obsolete when FIRE retires. After 1 January 2027, IRIS is the only electronic filing system for information returns, for the current year, prior years and corrections. Two earlier FIRE dates: 1 November is the last day to send test files to FIRE's test system, and 9 November the last day to change an existing FIRE application for a Transmitter Control Code (TCC). The IRS no longer accepts new FIRE TCC applications. Current FIRE users must apply for an IRIS TCC to file tax year 2026 returns in 2027.
entries.affected: Code that writes Publication 1220 files, and whoever uploads them to FIRE: in-house payables and payroll exports, and open-source writers such as moov-io/irs (a Go reader and writer for FIRE files, its latest commit, on 23 October 2026, was a dependency update) and sdj0/fire-1099 (Python, last commit in March 2022). IRIS has two ways in, and both use IRS formats of their own, not the Publication 1220 layout. The free Taxpayer Portal takes up to 100 returns at a time, typed in or uploaded as .csv using the IRS's templates. IRIS A2A takes XML from software (IRS Publication 5718); it needs an A2A TCC, an API client ID and successful test transmissions before you can file. We did not count how much code writes Publication 1220 files.
entries.check: From your repository root, search for the Publication 1220 format, FIRE addresses and the moov-io/irs library, as below. A match is worth reading, not proof: a file can describe the format without writing it. No match does not clear you, because a fixed-width writer may carry no such comment, so also ask who uploads your information returns at fire.irs.gov. Then check whether your organization already has an IRIS TCC: the IRS tells current FIRE users to apply for one, and an IRIS TCC can only be used for IRIS.

fix.text: Apply for an IRIS TCC now. IRS Publication 5903 says the typical application is processed within 45 business days, and it needs at least two Responsible Officials (one for a sole proprietorship, an S corporation or a single-member LLC). Forms 1099-NEC for 2026 are due at the IRS on 1 February 2027, because 31 January is a Sunday. By our count, skipping weekends and federal holidays, an application sent on 24 November 2026 reaches 45 business days on 1 February 2027, the due date itself, which leaves no time to file or, for A2A, to pass the tests; typical is the IRS's word, not a promise. Then choose a route: the Taxpayer Portal for up to 100 returns at a time, or IRIS A2A for software, after its tests. To correct a return first filed through FIRE, file the correction in IRIS: the IRS's August 2026 working-group slides add OtherIntakeSystemInd and OtherIntakeSystemNm (value "FIRE") to the IRIS schema for this, with details due in Publication 5718 and the tax year 2026 schema. We have not filed through IRIS ourselves.

entries.short: ubuntu-latest → 26.04: Java 25 can break Gradle
entries.title: GitHub moves ubuntu-latest to Ubuntu 26.04: the default Java becomes 25, and Gradle 8 builds that don't choose a JDK can fail
entries.what: As ubuntu-latest moves to Ubuntu 26.04 (19 October to 19 November 2026), the runner's default Java changes from 17 to 25. GitHub's announcement table still lists 17 as the 26.04 default; the 26.04 image readme lists 25.0.5 (both read 2 November). Java 8 is not installed on 26.04. Gradle officially supports Java 25 from 9.1.0.
entries.affected: Jobs on ubuntu-latest that run Gradle without choosing a JDK (no actions/setup-java step and no JAVA_HOME setting) and use a Gradle 8.x or older wrapper, or a Kotlin Gradle plugin 2.1.0 or older. That includes flutter build apk and appbundle, which run the project's Android Gradle wrapper and compile Kotlin. In our container tests, Gradle 7.6.4, 8.5, 8.13 and 8.14.3 failed on Temurin 25 and passed on Temurin 17. Gradle 8.14.4 to 8.14.6, the last 8.x releases, carry a partial Java 25 fix: on Temurin 25.0.5 they passed with a Groovy build script (build.gradle) and still failed with a Kotlin one (build.gradle.kts), which new Flutter and Android projects use. The Groovy pass holds only for projects that compile no Kotlin or use Kotlin Gradle plugin 2.1.10 or later: with plugin 1.9.25, 2.0.21 or 2.1.0, compileKotlin failed on Gradle 8.14.6, and 2.0.21 and 2.1.0 failed on 9.1.0 too. With a Groovy build script on Gradle 8.14.3 or older the error is "Unsupported class file major version 69"; with a Kotlin build script, "What went wrong" shows only the Java version, such as 25.0.5; with an older Kotlin Gradle plugin, compileKotlin prints "e: java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: 25.0.5". In a sample of 1,094 recently active Java, Kotlin and Dart repositories, about 1 in 70 of those that build JVM code on ubuntu-latest would hit this, most of them Flutter apps (predicted, not run). A Gradle cache restored from a 24.04 run can hide the failure until a build script changes.
entries.check: Run these at the repository root. entries.title: OpenAI shuts down its text-to-speech models, and its Speech endpoint has no model left to use
entries.what: On 1 October 2026 OpenAI announced that tts-1, tts-1-hd and gpt-4o-mini-tts (including the gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-03-20 and gpt-4o-mini-tts-2025-12-15 snapshots) will be removed from the API on 6 January 2027. entries.short: MySQL TIMESTAMP refuses dates after 2038
entries.title: MySQL TIMESTAMP columns already refuse dates after 19 January 2038
entries.what: A MySQL TIMESTAMP column holds times up to 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038, the largest second a signed 32-bit count can hold, and refuses any later value when it is written. So the limit applies now to every future date kept in such a column: since 20 January 2008 for a 30-year term that starts on the day it is written, and since 20 January 2023 for a 15-year one. On 4 November 2026, MySQL 9.7.4, the current long-term-support release, refused 2038-01-19 03:14:08 and 2040-01-01 00:00:00 with ERROR 1292 (22007): Incorrect datetime value; 8.4.13 did the same. With strict mode off (sql_mode set to an empty string), both stored 0000-00-00 00:00:00 instead, with only a warning.
entries.affected: Applications that keep future dates in a MySQL TIMESTAMP column: the end of a loan, lease, subscription or warranty, certificate and licence expiry, scheduled jobs and other "valid until" fields. A column that only records the current time, such as created_at, keeps working until 2038. MariaDB 11.5 and later on 64-bit builds hold TIMESTAMP values up to 2106-02-07; in our runs MariaDB 12.3.3 and 11.8.9 stored both dates. We tested the database alone, not any application built on it.
entries.check: Run this query in MySQL as root, or another account that can see every schema; it lists only the tables the account can see. It returns every TIMESTAMP column outside the system schemas, including columns of views: for a view, change the table behind it. For each column, ask whether it can ever hold a date after 19 January 2038. If inserts of such dates give no error but read back as 0000-00-00 00:00:00, the server is not in strict mode and is losing them without an error.
entries.checkCode:
SELECT table_schema, table_name, column_name
FROM information_schema.columns
WHERE data_type = 'timestamp'
  AND table_schema NOT IN ('mysql', 'sys', 'performance_schema', 'information_schema')
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;

fix.text: Change the column to DATETIME. Copy its definition from SHOW CREATE TABLE and change only the type: keep NOT NULL, DEFAULT, ON UPDATE, COMMENT and the precision (DATETIME(6) for TIMESTAMP(6)), because MODIFY drops whatever you leave out. Run it with the session time zone your application uses for this column, so the times it reads stay the same. At any other zone, the change moves every stored time with no error: in our test, an application at +05:30 read 12:00 before the change and 06:30 after it, because the change ran at UTC. Use UTC only if the application moves to UTC too. MySQL does not convert DATETIME between time zones, so from then on the column holds the application's clock time. The change copies the table and blocks writes while it runs. A table partitioned on UNIX_TIMESTAMP() of the column cannot be changed this way. Rows already stored as 0000-00-00 00:00:00 stay lost, and a strict session refuses the change until you repair them. Try it on a copy of the table first. On 9.7.4 and 8.4.13 the changed column kept the times the application read and its NOT NULL, DEFAULT and ON UPDATE; it took 2040-01-01 00:00:00 and dropped out of the check query.

entries.short: node:latest becomes Node 27
entries.time: planned release date; the tags move when the 27.0.0 images are published
entries.title: node:latest becomes Node 27, and node:latest and node:lts stop being the same image
entries.what: Node.js 27.0.0 is planned for 22 April 2027. Node 27 is the first release line under the new Node.js schedule: it has been in an alpha phase since October 2026 (the first alpha, 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0, is dated 29 October), and 27.0.0 makes it the Current release. In the official Docker image, the tags without a version number follow the Current release, so node:latest, node:current, node:slim, node:alpine, node:trixie, node:bookworm and their variants move from Node 26 to Node 27 once the 27.0.0 images are published. node:lts and node:26 stay on Node 26. node:latest and node:lts have been the same image since 28 October 2026; on 22 April they split. Node 26.0.0 came out on 5 May 2026 and its images were merged the next day; Node 24.0.0's images were merged on its release day, 6 May 2025. The image maintainers are rewriting their tag generator for the alpha phase in an open pull request (2681). We ran that version. With today's data it produces the same tags as the published list. With the Node 27 entry from the open pull request that adds the alpha images (2678), a 27.0.0 release added to the release list it reads, and the clock set to 21 April 2027, it moved no tags; with the clock set to 22 April it moved 18 tags to Node 27. Neither pull request is merged yet. The generator in use today, once rerun, would drop latest, current and the other tags without a version number from the list, leaving them on Node 26 until a fix is merged. The floating tags for the alpha period are still under discussion. An open issue (2680) proposes dropping or deprecating the current tags, and a reply argues against removing them from Node 26. A tag that is dropped from the list is not deleted from Docker Hub. It keeps its last image and stops getting updates, so node:current and the current- tags might stay on Node 26 instead of moving. Executed by us; not independently reproduced.
entries.affected: Dockerfile stages, Compose services and CI jobs whose image is node with no tag, node:latest, node:current, or another tag without a version number (node:slim, node:alpine, node:alpine3.24, node:alpine3.23, node:trixie, node:trixie-slim, node:bookworm, node:bookworm-slim, or a current- form such as node:current-slim), without an @sha256 digest. They get Node 27 the next time the machine fetches the image after the move: a fresh CI runner, docker pull, or docker build --pull. A machine that already has the image keeps Node 26 until it pulls again. Node 27's Linux variants can change before April. A tag for a variant Node 27 does not have stays on its last Node 26 image. Which changes break code will be in the 27.0.0 release notes, which are not out yet. The notes for the first alpha list several, among them: when --max-old-space-size is not set, the default heap limit becomes half of physical memory, between 256 MB and 4 GB, and memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer counts toward it; v8.serialize(), structuredClone() and postMessage() use a format that older Node.js releases cannot read; req.headers in the http module has a null prototype; npm moves to 12.1.0 and the bundled OpenSSL to 4.1.0. That list can change before 22 April. Tags with a version number, such as node:26-slim, do not move. The proposed alpha images get only exact version tags, such as 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0-trixie-slim. In that pull request no floating tag points at an alpha; the maintainers are discussing whether to add one, such as next.
entries.check: Run this from your repository root. It lists lines in Dockerfiles, Containerfiles and YAML files outside node_modules where FROM, image:, container: or an ARG line names node with no tag or with a tag that has no version number. It leaves out lines that name a major (node:26), lts, a release codename (node:iron, node:jod) or an @sha256 digest. Each line it prints is a candidate; check it. It also prints images named through a variable, such as node:${NODE_TAG}; read your ARG lines for those. It can print lines that are fine, such as an image whose name ends in node or a line that is commented out. It does not see GitLab's long form (image: then name: node:latest on the next line); search for name: node there. On our test files, run with GNU grep 3.12 in bash and dash, it printed every line it should, and its only extra lines were of the kinds named here.

fix.text: To stay on Node 26, name it: node:26, node:26-slim and node:26-alpine stay on Node 26, which Node.js supports until 30 April 2029, and node:lts stays on Node 26 until Node 27 becomes LTS, planned for 20 October 2027. To see what Node 27 changes for your code, run your tests on the Node 27 alpha before April; Node.js says alpha releases are for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production. We did not test whether a given project works on Node 27.

entries.title: Node 22 reaches end of life, and the node:22 images stop getting updates
entries.what: Node.js 22 (Jod) reaches end of life on 30 April 2027. Node.js says a release line at end of life no longer receives updates, security patches included. The official Docker image drops a release line from its build list at about that time: Node 20, which reached end of life on 30 April 2026, was dropped on 1 May 2026, and Node 18, end of life 30 April 2025, on 28 May 2025. The tags are not deleted: on 4 November 2026 Docker Hub still served node:20 and node:18, last updated on 22 April 2026 and 23 May 2025. So node:22 keeps pulling after it is dropped, but it is no longer rebuilt: no Node.js fixes and no Debian or Alpine package updates.
entries.affected: Dockerfile stages, Compose services and CI jobs on a node:22 tag (node:22, node:22-slim, node:22-alpine, node:22-bookworm and the like, or the codename tags node:jod and node:lts-jod), and CI setup steps, .nvmrc, .node-version and .tool-versions files that install Node 22, including by its name lts/jod. Nothing fails on 30 April itself: builds keep working, but security fixes released for newer Node.js lines after that date do not come to Node 22. node:22 and node:22-slim are Debian 12 (bookworm).
entries.check: Run this from your repository root. It lists lines that pick Node 22 in Dockerfiles, Containerfiles, YAML files, .nvmrc, .node-version and .tool-versions outside node_modules: node:22 and node:jod images, lts/jod, node-version: lines that name 22, and version files that start with 22. A version range in package.json, such as >=22, is not listed and does not need to change. It can print a range in a node-version: line, such as '>=22', which runs the newest matching Node.js already on the runner, or downloads the newest release if none matches; check those. It misses versions set through a variable; read your ARG and env lines too. On our test files, run with GNU grep 3.12 in bash and dash, it printed every line it should, and its only extra line was such a range.

fix.text: Move to Node 24, supported until 30 April 2028, or Node 26, supported until 30 April 2029, and run your own tests on it; we did not test whether a given project works there. node:24 and node:24-slim stay on Debian 12 and still include Yarn v1 and Corepack. node:26 images include neither, and node:26 and node:26-slim are Debian 13 (trixie), whose apt has no apt-key.
